4.summary: Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour
4.description: Lindsey Stirling brings her spectacular Snow Waltz Tour to State Farm Center this holiday season. The award-winning violinist, dancer and entertainer delivers a one-of-a-kind holiday experience featuring breathtaking choreography, stunning visuals and Lindsey’s genre-defying arrangements of holiday classics and original music. Blending classical violin with electronic, pop and rock influences, Stirling has created a live show unlike anything else — combining virtuosic musicianship with dance, theatrical production and aerial performance. Her annual holiday tour has become a seasonal tradition, bringing the music of her acclaimed Christmas albums Warmer in the Winter and Snow Waltz to life on stage. $1 per ticket goes towards Lindsey’s foundation, The Upside Fund, which focuses on equitable healthcare and medical debt relief, mental health access, and nutrition education and food justice.   Learn more about Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour

67.description: Not Mine Only Held.Join the Asian American Cultural Center for an Artist Showcase featuring Kuhu Shukla and her exhibition, Not Mine Only Held. The exhibition explores themes of identity, belonging, memory, and our connections to people, places, and culture. Drawing on Warli art, an ancient visual tradition of the Warli people of Maharashtra, India, Shukla uses its geometric language alongside influences from the Pacific Northwest to explore memory, myth, emotion, imagination, and our relationship with the natural world. Her work also draws on the story of Maa Sati and Shakti, reflecting on female power, gentle defiance, and the tribulations and triumphs of women across generations.Meet the artist, experience her work, and connect with our community at the opening reception.Location: Asian American Cultural Center, 1210 W. Nevada St., Urbana, ILThe exhibition will be on display from September 11 through December 11, 2026. This program is supported in part by the City of Urbana Arts Grant. This event is open to all eligible persons, regardless of race, color, or national origin.

Drawing on Warli art, an ancient visual tradition of the Warli people of Maharashtra, India, Shukla uses its geometric language alongside influences from the Pacific Northwest to explore memory, myth, emotion, imagination, and our relationship with the natural world. Her work also draws on the story of Maa Sati and Shakti, reflecting on female power, gentle defiance, and the tribulations and triumphs of women across generations.Meet the artist, experience her work, and connect with our community at the opening reception.Location: Asian American Cultural Center, 1210 W. Nevada St., Urbana, ILThe exhibition will be on display from September 11 through December 11, 2026. This program is supported in part by the City of Urbana Arts Grant. This event is open to all eligible persons, regardless of race, color, or national origin.

289.summary: Exhibition | Ink Shower: Contemporary Taiwanese Artists Reimagine Tradition
289.description: For more than a thousand years, ink painting has been a venerable practice, conveying people’s deepest beliefs and highest aspirations. Ink art has expressed complex, evolving ideas about aesthetics, spirituality, and the nature of the human condition. In today’s world, the range of visual and cultural concerns at the heart of ink art—developed into a major artistic tradition in China during the Tang dynasty (618–907)—now informs a wide range of art, including painting, sculpture, video, photography, animation, and more. Ink Shower focuses on dynamic works of art in this vein produced by twelve Taiwanese artists. While the cultural fabric of Taiwan has been shaped by waves of colonialism, modernization, and globalization, the tradition of ink art in Taiwan has never been a mere continuation of history. Instead, it has evolved through a process of cultural bricolage—appropriating and transforming elements to create new meanings. Rooted in the genealogy of Chinese ink traditions, ink art in Taiwan has been deeply intertwined with local artistic developments since the mid-twentieth century. Over time, the singular path of “ink as tradition” has been gradually dismantled through movements such as modern ink painting, nativist realism, and conceptual art. Taiwanese artists have come to regard ink not merely as a medium, but as a conceptual device and cultural signifier—shifting from medium to spirit, and from spirit to a renewed engagement with diverse media. Ink Shower does not assert a direct narrative. Rather, it adopts an oblique, mobile, and peripheral strategy—entering from the margins, unfolding from dim light, and transforming “ink” into a cultural tool for understanding identity, reimagining history, and envisioning the future. Situating “ink” as a mixture of aesthetic and cultural concerns rather than simply a medium, the exhibition incorporates a range of media to celebrate several distinctively Taiwanese contributions to this enduring and malleable tradition.
289.location: Krannert Art Museum | Main Level | East Gallery

403.summary: INHS Seminar | Milkweed Conservation Genetics: Prairie remnants and restorations
403.description: This seminar will be held in room 1005 Forbes Natural History Building, 1816 S. Oak Street, Champaign with a virtual Zoom option at https://illinois.zoom.us/j/82837070775?pwd=FpF57pLCabuqaIO5Y7qUBhkdPKyWbX.1&from=addon | Meeting ID: 828 3707 0775 | Password: 656969

404.description: Over the six years of 2013-2019, the Dark Energy Survey (DES) imaged one eighth of the sky, measuring the properties of hundreds of millions of galaxies. In 2026, the Vera Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) has begun a ten-year endeavor to to collect even more precise measurements of roughly 20 billion galaxies. In this talk I will discuss how we leverage galaxy iimaging data to probe the geometry and growth of structure in our Universe, and through that, to test models describing the physics of dark energy, dark matter, and gravity. I will present results from the recently released DES Year 6 cosmology analysis of galaxy clustering and weak gravitational lensing, and will highlight how, as the largest-area galaxy imaging survey of its kind, DES serves as a laboratory for preparation for analysis with next-generation cosmological experiments like the Vera Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST).

405.description: Join a collaborative group that will help you figure out what matters to you and offer support as you explore new paths that align with your values, skills, and interests. The group will involve hands-on exercises and rich conversation designed to guide you in claiming agency about your next steps, even amid challenging circumstances. Graduate students and postdocs in any field whose work involves humanistic inquiry, regardless of department, are welcome to participate.  Participants commit to meeting once a week for 3 weeks, with ~1 hour of additional work in between sessions. The Fall 2026 Humanities Career Discovery Group will meet in-person on Tuesdays, 3:30-5:00 PM from November 3 through November 17 at the Graduate College (507 E. Green St.). Registration is required. Register at https://go.grad.illinois.edu/HumanitiesCareerGroup. See the full listing of Graduate College workshops at https://go.grad.illinois.edu/workshops *If you require any disability-related accommodations to participate in this workshop more fully, please email gradsuccess@illinois.edu

406.summary: Getting Started with Fellowship and Proposal Writing
406.description: This presentation will provide an introduction to writing research statements for fellowship and grant proposals. You'll learn more about the statement's purpose in relation to other application materials, review common features, practice explaining the novelty and significance of your research, and gain tips for writing impactfully. Writers from any discipline are welcome, and this presentation will be most effective for students with limited fellowship and grant writing experience who are seeking to demystify the application process.This presentation will be held via Zoom, and is open to all current U of I affiliates (students, faculty, and staff). You will need to be logged into Zoom with your Illinois credentials to join. Please register with your Illinois email by November 9 to receive the Zoom details on the morning of the event. If you register on the day of, please email wow@illinois.edu immediately to request the Zoom details - we will do our best to get them to you prior to the event. All registrants will receive access to the presentation materials via email the following business day.

407.summary: Giving Thanks: Exploring Ontologies of Relationality
407.description: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois Confederacy) articulate a philosophy of gratitude and reciprocity through the Thanksgiving Address (Ohén:ton Karihwatéhkwen), often translated as “The Words That Come Before All Else.” In this Indigenous framework, Thanksgiving is not a single event but an ongoing, cyclical practice. By creating a dialogical space, this Dinner on Us program seeks to explore how gratitude, relational accountability, and respect for the diversity of life shape ways of knowing and being.
407.location: Asian American Cultural Center (1210 W. Nevada St., Urbana, IL 61801)

408.description: Interested in launching a startup in the United States but unsure how your international student status fits into the picture? The International Student Entrepreneurship Workshop is designed to help international students better understand the immigration policies and requirements that can affect starting and growing a business in the U.S.   Immigration attorney Matthew Meltzer of Meltzer Hellrung, LLC, who specializes in employment-based immigration and works with entrepreneurs and companies, will share practical guidance and answer student questions. Whether you already have a startup, are exploring an idea, or simply want to understand your options for pursuing entrepreneurship in the U.S., this workshop is a great opportunity to get informed and ask questions directly from an expert.

411.summary: ECHOES Across the Atlantic | APOLLO'S FIRE
411.description: Apollo’s Fire conductor and harpsichordist Jeannette Sorrell, praised as \"a master musical storyteller\"(Seen & Heard International, UK) and known for her compelling explorations of multicultural influences in early music, creates timely programs that ask us to ponder our shared history. As the Grammy-winning baroque ensemble returns to Krannert Center, legendary Trinidadian soprano Jeanine De Bique joins them to explore the historical connections between Europe and the Caribbean colonies in the 18th century. Across the waters, tales of love, despair, and resilience emerge from the palaces of Europe and the plantations of the Caribbean—with surprising resonance for today. The virtuoso music of Handel, Purcell, Rameau, and Vivaldi meets the soulful voices of Caribbean poets in this celebration of our shared humanity. Learn more about ECHOES Across the Atlantic | APOLLO'S FIRE

412.summary: Lyric Theatre @ Illinois: Singin' in the Rain
412.description: The \"Greatest Movie Musical of All Time\" is faithfully and lovingly adapted by Broadway legends Betty Comden and Adolph Green, from their original award-winning screenplay in Singin' in the Rain. Each unforgettable scene, song, and dance is accounted for, including the show-stopping title number, complete with an onstage rainstorm! Hilarious situations, snappy dialogue and a hit-parade score of Hollywood standards make Singin' in the Rain the perfect entertainment for any fan of the golden age of movie musicals. Learn more about Lyric Theatre @ Illinois: Singin' in the Rain

413.summary: Deerfield + University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign: Collaborating to Advance Biomedical Innovation
413.description: How do academic investigators work with investors to turn promising scientific ideas into real-world companies? Please join us for a conversation with the Deerfield team to explore their work in advancing academic innovation through Deerfield’s partnership with Illinois. Deerfield is an investment firm dedicated to advancing healthcare through investment, intelligence, and philanthropy. The firm's internal drug discovery and development group, 3DC, is a partner to various stakeholders in the biotech ecosystem, including principal investigators in Deerfield’s academic collaboration network, as well as startups, and biopharma companies. What you’ll learn:How Deerfield and 3DC partner with academic medical centers and aim to turn research and clinical ideas into real-world healthcare innovations and new biotech venturesWhat capabilities and resources Deerfield can bring to help enable productive partnerships with Illinois scientists and cliniciansWhat Deerfield’s areas of interest are for academic collaborations, and how to engageMembers of the Illinois biomedical ecosystem likely to find this most interesting:Faculty, students, and staff involved in translational researchClinicians and medical center leaders interested in industry collaborationsBiomedical innovation leaders and entrepreneurs SPEAKERS Nadim Shohdy, Ph.D., Chief Operating Officer, Deerfield Discovery and Development William Slattery, Partner, Therapeutics Investment Team
413.location: Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology, Room 5602

415.summary: Global Engagement Lounge (GEL) - Dating Across Cultures: Understanding & Navigating Differences
415.description: Navigating dating in a new culture can feel confusing and isolating, but you’re not alone. 423.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 438.summary: Ximing Cai, \"From Wishes to Actions – Reflections on Aspiration for International Water Resources Management\"
438.description: Ximing Cai, \"From Wishes to Actions – Reflections on Aspiration for International Water Resources Management\" Time: 12:00 pm, Tuesday, Nov 12, 2026 Location: Coble 306 and Zoom Abstract: Over the past 30 years, the world has seen no shortage of aspirations for international water resources management: water diplomacy promises cooperation across borders; virtual water trade suggests that food trade can alleviate local water pressures; SDG 6 establishes a global commitment to water and sanitation for all; and many other ambitious concepts and initiatives have emerged. Yet, evidence of successfully translating these aspirations into sustained action remains limited. This talk reflects on the persistent gap between aspiration and action, drawing on real-world efforts to implement these ideas, concerns raised by the water community, and Professor Cai’s thoughts on the barriers that stand in the way. It proposes a pathway of learning, adapting, and scaling up by pairing big ideas with operational pilots and engaging stakeholders through a shared-vision approach. Ultimately, however, even the best ideas and approaches cannot become reality without a collaborative world. About the speaker: Ximing Cai is the Ben Yen Professor of Civil and Environmental Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana–Champaign. His primary research area is water resources systems analysis, with a focus on coupled hydrology-human systems; his interdisciplinary work bridges hydrology and economics to unravel complex environmental and water-resources systems and to inform management policies. He was elected a Fellow of the American Geophysical Union (AGU) in 2019 for forging a new science of hydrologic change that accounts for human interactions and advances water-resources management, and a Fellow of the International Water Resources Association (IRWA) in 2024 for outstanding research and leadership in global water-resources management. He currently chairs IWRA’s Task Force on Downscaling th

445.summary: Navigating Complexity: Health Literacy as a Foundation for Health Equity
445.description: Please join the Health Technology Education Program for a presentation by James (Jay) Duhig at 5:15 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, in 3019 Huff Hall. Duhig leads AbbVie's Office of Health Literacy within Patient Safety, working to make medicine and clinical research information clearer, more usable and more meaningful for patients and other health care audiences. His experience spans health literacy, human factors, patient engagement, risk communication, regulatory affairs and medical devices. Duhig also serves on the advisory board for the MS program in Health Technology. Navigating Complexity: Health Literacy as a Foundation for Health Equity Health care has become increasingly complex, placing growing demands on people to find, understand, evaluate and use information to make decisions about their health. Drawing on lessons from a career spanning health literacy, patient safety, human factors, risk communication, patient engagement and regulatory science, James (Jay) Duhig explores in this lecture how health literacy can help people navigate that complexity. The lecture will examine the evolution of health literacy from a focus on individual understanding to a broader responsibility to design information, communications and health care experiences around the needs of the people they are intended to serve. It will also consider health literacy as a vital component of health equity, recognizing that everyone should have a meaningful opportunity to understand their choices, participate in decisions and navigate health care successfully. Ultimately, achieving health equity requires more than providing information. It requires creating environments in which all people can access, understand and use health information to make informed decisions that reflect their needs, values and circumstances.

459.summary: \"‘Imagining Capital in the City: Urban Life in DLF’s Public Projection, 1949-1960\", Anish Vanaik, Purdue University
459.description: Imagining Capital in the City: Urban Life in DLF’s Public Projection, 1949-1960Delhi Land and Finance (DLF), now India’s largest real estate firm, first muscled its way into Indian urban development in the late 1940s. About a decade later, Delhi’s Master Plan of 1961 - brought private land development to a close in the city. Between 1950 and 1960, however, DLF’s spurt of urban development was spectacularly successful, creating close to 30 ‘colonies’ in the rapidly expanding city. Among the distinctive elements of DLF’s activity in this period was a determined effort to build a public brand. This drew on a fascinating set of ambient ideas: a future of plenitude, a present of resilient response to emergency, reliable engineering and an unabashed embrace of urban modernity. Through a range of materials relating to DLF’s public projection, including advertisements, naming conventions and brochures, in English, Hindi and Urdu this paper reconstructs the elements of the early DLF brand. In the process, it argues, that we see the early presence of an imagining of city life in the aftermath of Partition that was quite distinct from bothDelhi’s own traditions and the modernity promised in the Master Plan.

466.summary: PhD Defense | Remote Sensing of Fluvial Dynamics in River Confluences and Meander Bends
466.description: Remote Sensing of Fluvial Dynamics in River Confluences and Meander Bends Accurately characterizing the spatial and temporal dynamics of river systems is important for water resources management. Traditional field methods are labor-intensive, susceptible to noise from flow fluctuations, difficult to repeat under varying hydrological conditions, and particularly challenging in large rivers over large spatial scales. Remote sensing methods provide unprecedented opportunities to observe river dynamics globally at high spatial resolution. The dissertation explores the potential of remote sensing data to investigate fluvial dynamics at river confluences and meandering rivers. The objectives of this dissertation are to: i) evaluate the spatial scales and rates of mixing downstream of river confluences using aerial imagery, ii) investigate the spatial and temporal variations in water surface profiles upstream of river confluences using data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite, and iii) evaluate changes in lateral water-surface profiles in bends of meandering rivers using SWOT data. The first study evaluates the average length scales, rates, and variability of lateral mixing downstream at 43 confluences for 150 events based on contrasts in gray‐scale intensity of confluent flows captured by aerial images. Only 45% of the events exhibit complete mixing over the length of the imaged downstream reach. The average dimensionless length scale (sd) of complete mixing is 7.4 times the downstream flow width and varies from sd = 1.1–26.3, but not all flows completely mix. A nonlinear spatial pattern of mixing, consistent with relations derived from shallow flow theory, reveals that mixing rates are substantially higher immediately downstream of confluences with most mixing occurring over sd < 15. 492.summary: Spurlock Sunday: Animal Stereotypes - The serpent deceived me, I’m innocent
492.description: Due to their dazzling patterns, vivid colors and sometimes deadly venom, snakes have both fascinated and frightened humans for millennia. So much so that snakes hold a rich and varied place in human culture and mythology, symbolizing medicine, wisdom, temptation, creation, and the eternal cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.   In Hindu mythology the serpent goddess Manasa possesses the power to harm with one eye and to heal with the other. In Greek mythology, serpents are associated with both Asclepius, the god of healing, and Hermes, who is responsible for guiding souls to the underworld. Egyptian pharaohs have worn emblems of snakes as a sign of sovereignty. And because snakes periodically shed their skin, many ancient cultures associate them with rebirth, reinvention of the Self, and the immortal spirits of beloved ancestors. This duality of meaning appears frequently in both mythology and religion.   In Western and Near Eastern mythologies, snakes are famously cast as a malicious force or as a deceptive adversary. The Abrahamic traditions famously introduce the serpent in the Garden of Eden as a deceiving temptress, blamed for humanity’s ‘fall’ from innocence into sin. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, it is a serpent that steals eternal youth from Gilgamesh. Each narrative, of course, created by and for humans.    What associations do you make with snakes? Do they evoke fear, awe, or fascination? If a largely negative association, is it rooted in something factual about these extraordinary creatures or merely something stereotypical you’ve been conditioned to believe about their character? And like the serpents of mythology, what dualities might you represent — in the eyes of others as well as your own?    Join us in art making to reflect on the various mythologies that feature serpents, as well as their personal meaning to you. Please come design and paint your own movable wooden snake or paper puppet! For further information on this event, contact Jeffrey Pegram at jk

510.summary: CLACS Speaker Series: Angharad Valdivia \"Emilia Pérez: A Perfect Case Study of the overlap of Latin American and Latinx Studies\"
510.description: On November 16th at 3pm in Coble Hall 306, Professor Emerita Angharad Valdivia will present \"Emilia Pérez: A Perfect Case Study of the overlap of Latin American and Latinx Studies.\"  This presentation explores the controversies surrounding the film Emilia Pérez (2024) produced in France about a Mexican narrative whose transnational implications included US Latinx.  In particular, and via a Media Studies theoretical approach, I examine issues of visibilization of the trans main character and trans medical tourism, the country of Mexico, and AfroLatinidad as well as the policing of US Latinx Spanish language usage and the promise of counternarratives for highlighting the neocolonial gaze. Angharad N. Valdivia is Research Professor Emerita at the University of Illinois. Her research includes gender and the press in revolutionary Nicaragua, Latin American and Latinx popular cultural studies, girls studies, especially quinceañeras, and Disney Studies. She just published (Re)Booting Inequality: Critical Takes on Film and Television with Isabel Molina-Guzmán and Quinceañeras: Latinidades & Girlhood in Popular Culture with Jillian Báez and Diana Leon-Boys. Emilia Perez: Confronting the impossibility of authenticity (with Stephanie Pérez) is forthcoming. She is a Fellow of the International Communication Association and a Distinguished Scholar of the National Communication Association.

513.description: The European Union Center is proud to present the Urbana Opera Ensemble as the perform excerpts from \"The Mariage of Figaro\" at 6:30 pm on Monday, November 16.     The Urbana Opera Ensemble is a collective of local musicians whose were brought together by their passion for opera. Hailing from several different departments on campus, this supergroup is bringing excerpts from Mozart's \"The Mariage of Figaro.\" to the Knight Auditorium stage.     Performed in Italian, this four Act Opera tells the story of the drama filled wedding day of servants, Figaro and Susanna. As they prepare for their nuptials, their employer, the Count, attempts to seduce Susanna and marry off Figaro to a rich woman old enough to be his mother. With disguises, mistaken identities, hiding in closets, and lost signet rings, the opera arrives at its farcical climax when the Count and Susanna work together to reveal the Count's duplicity publicly in order to shame him and ultimately bring him to justice. The couple, Figaro and Susanna,  is happily married at the end of the opera.      Celebrate the comedy, heartbreak, and romance of the classic opera with the EUC and The Urbana Opera Ensemble.

530.summary: INHS Seminar | Ecology, Evolution, and Conservation of Island Boas
530.description: This seminar will be held in room 1005 Forbes Natural History Building, 1816 S. Oak Street, Champaign with a virtual Zoom option at https://illinois.zoom.us/j/82837070775?pwd=FpF57pLCabuqaIO5Y7qUBhkdPKyWbX.1&from=addon | Meeting ID: 828 3707 0775 | Password: 656969 Abstract: Islands are central to the biology, evolution, and conservation of the boas (superfamily Booidea) on a global scale. Of the 66 currently recognized species, 42 (63.6%) occur on islands and 27 (40.9%) are insular endemics. Four genera and two families are wholly insular, and a third family is predominantly so. I will discuss the biogeography, morphology, ecology, and conservation of boas globally, focusing on body-size evolution. Insular boas display the classic island syndrome of repeated, independent dwarfism and gigantism, exemplified by convergent dwarfing in continental-island Boa constrictor and the diverse radiation of 14 species of West Indian Boas. However, island boas are also highly susceptible to range contraction and extirpation, as seen in West Indian species.

533.summary: From Winds to Explosions: The Physics of Interacting Cool Giants
533.description: Rich in dust and heavy elements, the massive outflows of cool giant stars play a key role in the chemical evolution of galaxies and supply the raw material for planetary systems and life. Yet the origin of these outflows remains poorly understood. High-resolution observations have revealed highly complex circumstellar environments marked by spirals, shells, arcs, jets, and disks. The structures not only hold clues to the physical processes that drive and shape the outflows but are also important for understanding the mass-loss histories and final fates of these systems. Using advanced numerical codes with realistic microphysics, hydrodynamics, and radiative processes, we model these systems in full 3D, following matter from the stellar atmosphere through the circumstellar envelope to the interstellar medium. In this talk, I will focus on the impact of stellar and sub-stellar companions on cool giant outflows. I will discuss Wind Roche-Lobe Overflow (WRLOF), a mode of binary mass transfer that is efficient even in wide binaries and its implications for chemically peculiar stars, X-ray binaries, novae, and the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae. I will also show that companions as small as a few tens of Jupiter masses can sculpt the winds and enhance mass loss. On larger scales, bow shocks and detached shells form where the outflows collide with the interstellar medium. These structures subsequently affect the evolution of e.g., interacting supernovae, and the dust and gas that is ultimately returned to galaxies.

535.summary: Ukrainian Studies Lecture: \"From Documentation to Accountability: The Truth Hounds Experience\"
535.description: What can a civil society organization actually do to advance accountability for international crimes? Drawing on more than a decade of Truth Hounds’ work in Ukraine, this talk will examine how documentation can be transformed into investigations, legal analysis, case-building, and engagement with national and international justice mechanisms. It will explore the interaction between Ukrainian proceedings, the International Criminal Court, foreign jurisdictions, and quasi-judicial mechanisms, and how civil society can strategically navigate this “accountability multiverse” to turn information about atrocities into opportunities for truth and justice. The talk will also reflect on the challenges of sustaining accountability work amid increasingly unsustainable patterns of funding allocation and broader geopolitical turbulence.  Dmytro Koval is Chair of International and European Law at the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy, co-CEO at Truth Hounds. He has been a research fellow at Stanford University, Central European University, Jagiellonian University, and the Graduate School for Social Research of the Polish Academy of Science. He has lectured at Yale University, Stanford University, Mississippi College, Universidad Mayor de San Andrés of Bolivia, Royal Academy of Belgium, Jagiellonian University, Universidad Panamericana, University of Zurich. Dmytro served as a member of the Ministry of Justice Expert Committee on International Humanitarian Law Implementation. He consulted numerous NGOs on IHL and IHRL implementation in Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, China, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Ukraine. He also advised the Council of Europe, the European Parliament, UNESCO, the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Culture, the Prosecutor General’s Office, and Ukrainian MPs on different aspects of foreign policy and international law. 543.summary: Behind Ancient Bars: Narratives of Incarceration in the Hebrew Bible
543.description: Behind Ancient Bars: Narratives of Incarceration in the Hebrew Bible Presented by Hadar AviramThis event is free and open to the public.About the Book In Behind Ancient Bars, law professor and rabbinical student Hadar Aviram challenges the conventional assumption that incarceration is an artifact of modernity by looking back to depictions of detention and confinement in the Hebrew Bible. Aviram takes readers on a journey through the Hebrew Bible's carceral landscape through creative rereadings of five stories: Joseph in Egypt, Esther in Persia, Daniel in Babylonia, Samson in Gaza, and Jeremiah in Jerusalem. Drawing on her experience as a leading voice against mass incarceration, she finds connections between antiquity and the contemporary understanding of incarceration that encompasses not just the prison itself but also other confinement programs. Infusing ancient biblical stories with fresh life through modern punishment theories, Aviram shows how incarceration has much to teach us about government, the experience of people in confinement, and the strength and resilience of the human spirit across millennia.About the Author Hadar Aviram is the Thomas Miller '73 Professor at University of California College of the Law, San Francisco, and a rabbinic student at Hebrew Union College. She is the author of five books on punishment and incarceration and has published extensively about correctional policy, prison conditions, parole and release, and forgiveness. The former President of the Western Society of Criminology, Aviram is a frequent speaker on matters of prison conditions, and as part of her pro-bono work was part of the legal team who litigated on behalf of San Quentin prisoners during the COVID-19 pandemic. Her fourth book recounting that experience, FESTER (with Chad Goerzen), won the American Society of Criminology book award in 2025. Behind Ancient Bars is her fifth book, a synergy between her decades of experience in prison scholarship and her newer research

552.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 562.summary: Book Launch | Forgive Us Our Debts: How Black Churches Use Bankruptcy to Survive
562.description: Please join us for a book launch for \"Forgive Us Our Debts: How Black Churches Use Bankruptcy to Survive,\" featuring a panel discussion among experts in the bankruptcy field and commentary from author Pamela Foohey (University of Minnesota Law School). About the Book When American churches face financial difficulties, a disproportionately high number of Black churches reorganize under chapter 11 bankruptcy. There are no easy explanations for this distinction: not location, denomination, leadership structure, or the reasons for the loans. Forgive Us Our Debts details why, then, Black churches account for two-thirds of all congregations that file for chapter 11 bankruptcy every year. Drawing on case studies of six Black churches and one white church, and 150 interviews with church leaders, members, and attorneys, it situates the answer in a long history of predatory lending and bankruptcy law's power to help churches work with recalcitrant lenders to save their spiritual homes and keep their doors open. This event is free and open to the public. Lunch will be provided (while supplies last).Panelists Moderator: Ralph Brubaker University of Illinois College of LawJudge Jim Carr U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of IndianaRobert Lawless University of Illinois College of LawJennifer Robbennolt University of Illinois College of LawCommentaryPamela Foohey University of Minnesota Law School This event is part of Illinois DREAMS (Bankruptcy Day) at the College of Law. Please join us for our next seminar: Speaker: Prof. DeLisa FairweatherDate: Thursday, November 19, 2026Time: 12:00 PM – 1:00 PMLocation: Room 3269 - 3rd floor Tower Room, Beckman InstituteTitle: The Yin and Yang of EVs in myocardial inflammation About the Speaker: Dr. DeLisa Fairweather is Professor of Medicine and Consultant in the Departments of Cardiovascular Medicine and Immunology at Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida. 568.summary: Brown Bag Series - Seeking (and making) refuge in, out of, and beyond Europe: An ethnography of world-making
568.description: Abstract: This presentation leverages the life history of an individual whose multiple displacements and emplacements in, out of, and beyond Europe in the last decade of the 20th century offer opportunities to explore the lived and experiential of dimensions of seeking and finding refuge in modern times. This multi-sited account of uprootedness and re-rootedness helps relativize a jural category, namely the Convention refugee, by advancing a notion of refuge as continuum. The analysis will invite a shift of the analytical direction toward fluidity, performativity, and practice, and away from the rigidity of bureaucratically crafted knowledge that categorizes, classifies, and constitutes 'the refugee' as a legal construct. Bio: Fethi Keles is a cultural anthropologist specializing in the ethnographic study of forced migration, refugees, and displacement with a focus on the experiences of Bosnian diaspora. He is currently a Fellow in the 2026-2027 cohort of the Weatherhead Scholars Program at the Weatherhead Center for International Affairs at Harvard University.

572.description: Jodi Melamed is professor of English and Race, Ethnic, and Indigenous Studies at Marquette University. She is the author of Represent and Destroy: Rationalizing Violence in the New Racial Capitalism (Minnesota UP, 2011), co-editor of Economies of Dispossession: Indigeneity, Race, Capitalism (with Jodi A. Byrd, Alyosha Goldstein, and Chandan Reddy), a special issue of the journal Social Text. Her influential essay, “Racial Capitalism,” is among the most cited articles in the journal Critical Ethnic Studies. Byrd, Alyosha Goldstein, and Chandan Reddy), “The Spirit of Neoliberalism: From Racial liberalism to neoliberal multiculturalism,” “Using Liberal Rights to Enforce Racial Capitalism” (with Chandan Reddy) and “ Don’t Arrest Me, Arrest the Police: Policing as the Street Administration of Colonial Racial Capitalism” (with Lisa Cacho). 574.description: Join us as we bring one of C-U's powerhouse voices to Krannert Center Uncorked on November 19! J'Lyn Hope is a multidisciplinary artist whose work explores the transformative power of imagination. Blending jazz, rock, soul, and improvisation, she creates dynamic musical experiences that blur the boundaries between sound, feeling, and discovery. Known for her expressive voice and magnetic energy, Hope uses her loop station to build intricate layers of music in real time, transforming her voice into rhythm, melody, harmony, and texture. She describes these creations as \"sound paintings\"—where the color of her voice follows the brushstrokes of her creativity. Her work is rooted in the belief that art is a powerful tool that encourages us to reach beyond our notions of what is possible, tapping into the magic of what lies beyond. The love, light, and hope infused throughout her art awaken the dreamer in us all. Come see J'Lyn Hope November 19 at Stage 5 in the Krannert Center lobby. Enjoy a beverage from our Stage 5 bar and connect with friends old and new. All Krannert Center Uncorked performances are free on select Thursdays from 5:30-7pm. 636.summary: Nutrition for Cats: Rethinking the Basics
636.description: Nutrition for Cats: Rethinking the Basics  We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas.  Date: Tuesday, December 1, 2026  Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online Webinar     Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas is a Brazilian veterinarian, professor, researcher, and specialist in companion animal nutrition. She earned her DVM, Master’s, and PhD in Animal Nutrition and Production from the School of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Science of the University of São Paulo (FMVZ-USP), with a strong focus on companion animal nutrition. Her professional experience spans clinical nutrition, small animal medicine, university teaching, scientific research, and technical training in the pet food industry. She currently serves as a university professor in Brazil and is the Director of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital at UNINTA Fortaleza. Cats have unique nutritional requirements that are often misunderstood or oversimplified. In this session, Dr. Rentas will revisit the foundations of feline nutrition, discuss common misconceptions, and examine how modern research is influencing approaches to long-term feline health and wellbeing. Sign up for the mailing list to receive the webinar link and updates.https://go.illinois.edu/ipets-webinars

654.summary: Food For Thought | Kimberly Mack and Laura Hetrick
654.description: Food for Thought: A series of public events featuring research and creative projects by recent CAS Associates and Fellows. We are delighted to showcase the work of some of our most productive and creative faculty in this informal series of intellectually and spiritually invigorating presentations. You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty.11:00am-11:45am: Kimberly Mack, CAS Associate 2025-26, English During her appointment as a CAS Associate, Kimberly Mack made considerable progress on a proposal and sample chapters for her critical memoir, Brown Sugar Blues: The White Soundtrack of a Black Girl Who Loves Rock. Brown Sugar Blues tells the story of how rock music both empowered and alienated Mack while growing up in a violent and musical home. It braids memoir, biography, and cultural criticism together to explore the personal and historical impacts of the erasure of Black people from rock—a style of music with Black origins. In this lecture, Mack considers the reasons and costs of Black women’s erasure from rock through the analysis of a controversial song that engages Black women and race, sex, power, and violence more directly than perhaps any other 1970s-era rock tune: “Brown Sugar” by the Rolling Stones. She tells the story of her mom’s uncritical love of the song, as well as her unwitting participation in her mom’s fandom, as a toddler, in 1971. Alongside this conversation about “Brown Sugar” is the story of how rock music helped Mack to bond with her mom while it simultaneously, due to its sexism and racism, complicated her budding awareness of her sexuality as a young Black girl. Noon-12:45pm: Laura Hetrick, CAS Associate 2025-26, Art + Design Beyond Voice: Reclaiming Neurodivergent Subjectivity as Knowers, Storytellers, and Scholars During a recent Center for Advanced Study appointment, Laura Hetrick completed drafts of two book-length projects that center neurodivergent voices and experiences. About the speakers John L. Anderson ('69, M.S., '71, Ph.D., Chemical Engineering) was president of the National Academy of Engineering (NAE) from 2019-25. 662.summary: 'How (not) to Kill a Language: The Many Lives of Sumerian'
662.description: The Sumerian language has lived many lives. It first lived more than 5,000 years ago on the streets and in the homes of the people of modern day Iraq. Sumerian experienced a new way of living when it became the subject of writing, when the language was used to record not only how much beer moved from one place to another, but eventually the legends of kings, the praise of goddesses, the recipes to recovering health, and the lullabies of a mother. But eventually, Sumerian suffered from time and political shifts; its speakers ceased teaching their children. But in its dying breath, Sumerian was given a new life, a new purpose: the language was resuscitated as the language of an ancient past, the language taught to the schoolchildren who might one day wield power, the language used to create histories and shape ideas. It became a language of access: to culture, to power, to the gods. And even long after it finally breathed its last 2,000 years ago as its life support — writing — finally gave out, it was once again reincarnated through Victorian decipherment and modern academics and fantasy storytellers. In her recent book How to Kill a Language, the journalist Sophia Smith Galer tells the stories of languages killed through neglect, premeditation, and abuse. The story of Sumerian is a different story; a story of how a language breathes when afforded new lives.

684.description: Handel’s Messiah remains one of the most enduring and beloved works in the choral repertoire, offering a profound synthesis of musical beauty and spiritual reflection. From the celebratory brilliance of the “Hallelujah” chorus to the introspective lyricism of its arias, Messiah traverses a wide emotional and theological landscape. Its carefully crafted structure and expressive clarity exemplify Handel’s dramatic genius. This performance invites audiences to engage with a work that continues to inspire through its balance of grandeur, intimacy, and a timeless holiday message. Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: Handel's Messiah

You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty.11:00am-11:45am: Tess McNulty, CAS Fellow 2025-26, English  Content Culture: The Forms of the Viral Era For almost two decades, we’ve been living in the era of viral content, from listicles to AI slop. But while much academic work has addressed this new media as information (conveying facts) or communication (coalescing communities), far less has considered its operations as imaginative, aestheticized entertainment. In this talk, Professor McNulty presents work from a book project that provides the first overarching cultural history of viral content from an aesthetic perspective, defining what she calls this new media's five major genres and interpreting the significance of their ubiquity. Noon-12:45pm: Alex Shakar, CAS Associate 2019-20, English Play the Void, a novel A mutant mushroom virus has jumped tracks to spark a human pandemic. A fateful presidential election looms. And the legendary singer Vic Vibes has been found dead. Now, an uncanny impersonator, Vic Voids, leads a chameleonic music tour across the land. Its mission: “unite the vibes” by playing to all sides of an increasingly violent culture war and topping one musical chart after another. But who’s behind the tour and to what ends? Why is a trove of Vic’s secrets pouring out: a tale shadowed by a crime, a love, and a nation’s troubled history? And who—or what—is Voids? In this talk, Professor Shakar will read from and discuss his forthcoming novel.
707.location: Levis Faculty Center, Room 208, 919 W Illinois St

712.summary: Planetary Architectures and Insights Towards Planet Formation
712.description: After a brief discussion about the types of exoplanetary architectures discovered so far, I will focus on one sub-population and what we can learn about planet formation by studying it in depth. Hot Jupiters were long thought to be lonely planets. This correctly describes the majority of the population and strongly motivates high-eccentricity tidal migration as the most common method of taking a hot Jupiter to its final short-period orbit. However, a growing number of systems now reveal nearby planetary companions. In this talk, I will discuss recent theoretical and observational results exploring the origin and evolution of hot Jupiters, with a particular focus on those with adjacent companion planets. I show that high-eccentricity tidal migration is generally incompatible with the survival of close-in companions except in very particular scenarios. I further demonstrate that while inner companions are dynamically robust, outer companions can be driven out of the transiting plane through secular interactions, stellar evolution, and stellar obliquity, potentially explaining their apparent absence in some systems. With this in mind, I present the discovery and characterization of the TOI-4468 system as a case study, highlighting how its unique architecture (an outer companion planet, but no inner companion) constrains its dynamical history. The full observational evidence suggests that while most isolated hot Jupiters likely formed through tidal migration, systems with nearby companions preferentially assembled in dynamically cold, disk-mediated ways, revealing multiple formation pathways for close-in giant planets.

713.summary: Alumni Lecture: Batamaka Somé, \"\"Pillars of Resilience: Rural Women’s Leadership and Farmer-Centered Research for Food System Transformation in the West African Sahel\"
713.description: International Year of the Woman Farmer Series hosted by the Center for the Study of Global Gender Equity and the College of ACES Office of International Programs welcomes Illinois Alumnus Batamaka Somé, PhD in Anthropology with a Graduate Minor in Gender Relations and International Development will give a talk titled \"Pillars of Resilience: Rural Women’s Leadership and Farmer-Centered Research for Food System Transformation in the West African Sahel\".  The December 8th talk will take place at 4:00pm in 210 Levis Faculty Center and via Zoom Conventional agricultural research has too often positioned farmers as recipients and adopters of technologies developed elsewhere, rather than as active partners in generating knowledge and shaping innovation. At the same time, persistent gender inequalities and patriarchal structures have constrained women’s voice and decision-making power in households, communities, and agricultural systems—despite the central roles rural women play in farming and across food systems. In this lecture, I draw on experiences from the West African Sahel to demonstrate the empowering potential of research grounded in farmers’ realities, priorities, and knowledge. More importantly, I showcase how rural women are leveraging farmer-centred research, alongside their own transformative leadership, to strengthen resilience and drive food system transformation. Against a backdrop of insecurity, climate variability, and geopolitical volatility, these experiences reveal rural women not simply as beneficiaries of agricultural development, but as agents of innovation, leaders of change, and essential pillars of resilient food systems in the Sahel.
713.location: 210 Levis Faculty Center and via Zoom

756.summary: Quick Start Workshop: Using the Pope Tech Accessibility Tool
756.description: Get up to speed on using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide to make Canvas pages more accessible for everyone! In this hands-on workshop, we’ll start with an overview of the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide, how it functions, what the various errors, alerts, structural elements, and features mean, and how to fix these issues on a Canvas page. 836.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Celebrate the body as an instrument with Step Afrika!, the GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS™ title holder for the Largest Stepping Dance and the world’s leading authority on the art form of stepping. The company’s newest work, The Fruits of Our Labor, blends the power of body percussion and contemporary dance with the vibrant energy of isipantsula (a rhythmic dance originating in South African townships) and the South African gumboot dance. Long-time Step Afrika! collaborator Jakari Sherman and South African choreographer Vusi Mdoyi lead an ensemble of virtuosic dancers whose bodies become instruments—clapping, striking, and stepping in mesmerizing unison, merging rhythm and ritual, history and storytelling. Recommended for grades 3 and up Learn more about School Performance: Step Afrika! presents The Fruits of Our Labor (KCYS)

840.summary: The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench
840.description: The Chicago-based Neo-Futurists have been writing and performing 30 plays in 60 minutes since 1988. Each play offers something different: be it funny, profound, elegant, disgusting, topical, irreverent, terrifying, or a song, all are original and truthful, tackling the here-and-now, and inspired by the lived experiences of the performers. “The ingenuity and engagement of the work not only remains but has deepened . . . the ensemble maps thorny social, psychological, and political terrain with foolishness and ferocity,” says the Chicago Reader. With new plays every week, The Infinite Wrench is The Neo-Futurists’ ongoing and ever-changing attempt to shift the conventions of live performance and speak to those unreached or unmoved by traditional theatre. Learn more about The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench

871.summary: Mark Morris Dance Group and Music Ensemble: Music at Play
871.description: With wit, exuberance, and an irresistible sense of play, the Mark Morris Dance Group brings together four works that showcase the humor, invention, and musical imagination of Mark Morris. Designed to delight audiences of all ages, this lively program combines brilliant dancing, vivid musicality, and theatrical surprise. In My Party, Morris transforms the familiar awkwardness and excitement of a youthful gathering into a tender and funny celebration of dancing together. The wonderfully offbeat Tamil Film Songs in Stereo Pas de Deux is pure cosmic invention propelled by the rhythms of South Indian popular music. Peccadillos, set to Erik Satie's miniature piano pieces originally written for children, finds humor and humanity in a whimsical solo filled with gesture, character, and imagination. And in Sport, Morris takes inspiration from Satie's playful Sports et divertissements, turning golf, swimming, tennis, and other athletic pursuits into a witty choreographic playground. Together, these four works offer an ideal evening of the Mark Morris Dance Group: sophisticated without being solemn, playful without ever losing artistry, and animated throughout by Morris' extraordinary ability to make music visible through dance. It is a program for longtime dance lovers, first-time audiences, children, parents, grandparents—and anyone who enjoys the pleasure of watching remarkable dancers have some serious fun. Learn more about Mark Morris Dance Group and Music Ensemble: Music at Play

880.description: Landscapes in Sound and Ink explores the rich dialogue between Taiwanese visual art and music. Presented in conjunction with the Ink Shower exhibition at the Krannert Art Museum and produced in collaboration with the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies, this program brings together works inspired by landscape, memory, nature, and cultural identity.  Featuring music by Taiwanese composers for piano trio and solo piano, the concert reflects the poetic atmosphere of ink painting traditions through sound, evoking mountains, water, mist, and shifting emotional landscapes. Through the interplay of visual art and music, audiences are invited to experience how musical textures and colors parallel the expressive brushwork and spatial imagination found in Taiwanese ink paintings. This collaborative event celebrates Taiwan’s artistic heritage while fostering cross-cultural understanding through music and visual art. This event is free to attend. Musicians Chi-Chen Wu, piano; Sam Ou, cello, Yu-Kun Hsiang, violin-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Free speech and academic freedom are foundational to our university’s missions of discovery and exploration. 891.summary: Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose
891.description: Join performer and educator, Seth Stewart, as he shares valuable and relatable lessons he’s learned in his journey to a successful career as an actor, dancer, choreographer, and leading performing arts educator. Audience questions will be welcomed during a Q&A session following Stewart’s talk. Stewart was an original cast member of Hamilton and performed in other Broadway shows including Sweet Charity and In the Heights. He has toured the world with popular artists such as Madonna, Jennifer Lopez, Mariah Carey, and more; appeared in movies like Sex and the City: The Movie and Music and Lyrics; as well as choreographed for the television show Bull, the Nickelodeon Kids’ Choice Awards, among others. In 2025, Stewart published his first book, Follow Your Vision, Live Your Truth, a memoir chronicling his journey from Broadway to a decade-long transformational spiritual journey that led him back to nature and his heart. Today, he serves as a performance coach and guest speaker through his company, Performer’s Edge, which provides coaching, courses, and workshops for pre-professional and professional artists – giving them the tools to succeed in the entertainment industry. Stewart is also the founder of True Kings Academy, a mentorship program supporting men with leadership skills through spiritual embodiment, mental health wellness, and wealth mindset. This event is sponsored by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs. Learn more about Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose

892.description: On Thursday, February 4th we will hear from Nini Zhou, Ph.D. Student in the College of Media at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Becoming Neoliberal Subjects: Algorithmic Governance of Feminist Activism in China\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.   In this talk, Nini Zhou discusses how algorithmic governance shapes feminist activism and produces neoliberal subjectivity in China. While existing scholarship has examined how neoliberal logics are embedded in feminist activism in China (Liu, 2023; Peng, 2021; Yin, 2022), less attention has been paid to how neoliberal logics embedded in technological structures shape feminist activism. To address this gap, this project focuses on how algorithmic governance in China structures visibility, participation, and value of feminist activism, thereby producing self-governing subjects. Algorithmic governance here refers to platform mechanisms functioning as infrastructures of digital governance, including content recommendation, search ranking, hashtag moderation, and traffic distribution. These mechanisms not only shape what content becomes visible, whose voices are amplified, and which forms of feminist expression are permitted or suppressed, but also produce regulatory frameworks for user practices in feminist activism.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

897.summary: Louie Palu | The Idea of North in Literature and Photography
897.description: Palu’s talk centers on distinct representations of the Arctic in literature and the visual arts, exploring this often-misunderstood region as both imagined otherworld and real-life landscape. Palu is especially interested in how texts such as John Milton’s epic Paradise Lost (1667) and Mary Shelley’s novel Frankenstein (1818) imagine the Arctic in the early decades of polar exploration, creating literary topographies which impact subsequent work not only in literature but the visual arts as well, including Palu’s ﬁlm and photography. Across these various media, Palu shows how inherited notions of the Arctic shape present-day discourses on subjects including climate change, resource extraction, indigenous rights, colonialism, and the militarization of polar territory. Hosted by: Department of English In conjunction with: American Indian Studies Program, College of Fine & Applied Arts, Creative Writing Program, Department of Anthropology, Department of Climate, Meteorology & Atmospheric Sciences, Department of Communication, Department of Earth Science & Environental Change, Department of Geography, Department of History, Department of Journalism, Department of Media & Cinema Studies, Humanities Research Institute, Krannert Art Museum, Russian, East European & Eurasian Center, School of Art + Design
897.location: Levis Faculty Center, Room 210, 919 W Illinois St

898.description: Acclaimed bassist Edgar Meyer, mandolin virtuoso Mike Marshall, and composer-violinist George Meyer unite as “Meyer, Marshall, Meyer” for an evening of inventive, genre-crossing music. A MacArthur Fellow and multiple Grammy Award winner, Edgar Meyer is widely regarded as one of the leading bassists of his generation, known for his work across classical, bluegrass, and contemporary music. Mike Marshall, a three-time Grammy nominee, has released more than 40 recordings and is celebrated for his fluency across bluegrass, jazz, classical, and Brazilian traditions. George Meyer brings a distinctive compositional voice shaped by both classical and fiddle traditions, with commissions and performances spanning major festivals and venues nationwide. Together, these longtime collaborators revisit and expand the repertoire of Edgar Meyer’s landmark project Short Trip Home, along with new works written for this ensemble, blending their individual and collective talents in an extraordinary program. Learn more about Meyer, Marshall, Meyer

922.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, February 11th we will hear from Felisa Reynolds, Associate Professor in Department of French and Italian at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Maryse Condé: Gender, and the Racial Logic of Francophone Classification \" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  This presentation draws from Dr. Reynolds' book project French or Francophone Literature: The Legacy of the Manifesto for a World Literature (Edinburgh University Press, forthcoming), which examines why the distinction between French and Francophone literature remains stubbornly intact twenty years after the publication of the manifest Pour une littérature-monde (“For a World Literature in French”), and what that persistence reveals about the racial logic organizing literary consecration in France. The chapter on Maryse Condé, which this presentation examines in detail, focuses on the reception of her work within the French literary field and argues that her decades-long exclusion from the Nobel Prize in Literature and from the highest echelons of French literary recognition was not incidental but structural, organized by the intersection of race and gender in ways that the field has never been asked to name, let alone justify.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

943.summary: Sinfonia da Camera: From Brahms with Love
943.description: Celebrating Valentine’s weekend, this program centers on the music of Johannes Brahms, whose works embody warmth, lyricism, and profound emotional depth. Alongside his music, Clara Schumann’s Konzertsatz in F Minor offers a compelling opening, reflecting her distinctive voice as both composer and pianist, as well as her close and deeply intimate artistic friendship with Brahms. Brahms’s Hungarian Dances (Nos. 1, 3, and 10) bring vibrant energy and rhythmic vitality, drawing on folk traditions with characteristic refinement. At the heart of the program, the Double Concerto in A Minor, performed by violinist Lucia Lin and cellist Owen Young, unfolds as an intimate musical dialogue of two voices in expressive conversation. The concert concludes with Brahms’s Symphony No. 2 in D Major, a radiant and expansive work whose pastoral beauty offers a luminous and deeply affectionate close. Program: Clara Schumann: Konzertsatz in F Minor for piano and orchestra Ian Hobson, piano and conductor Johannes Brahms: Hungarian Dances Nos. 1, 3, and 10 Johannes Brahms: Double Concerto in A Minor, Op. 102 Lucia Lin, violin; Owen Young, cello Johannes Brahms: Symphony No. 2 in D Major, Op. 73 Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: From Brahms with Love

955.summary: Seminar Series - Professor Brenda Wilson, Dept. of Microbiology
955.description: Beyond the Point-of-No-Return - Designer Toxin-Mediated Biothreats Bio: Brenda Anne Wilson, Ph.D., is a professor of microbiology and the Associate Director of Undergraduate Education in the School of Molecular & Cellular Biology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). She holds joint appointments in pathobiology at the College of Veterinary Medicine and in biomedical and translational sciences at the Carle Illinois College of Medicine. She is the Illinois Faculty Fellow for Sandia National Laboratories in the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Innovation.   After completing her B.A. in biochemistry and German from Barnard College at Columbia University, she was a DAAD graduate fellow of biochemistry at the Ludwig-Maximilians Universität München in Germany, studying virus labeling for in vivo tracking. She then earned her M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in chemistry from the Johns Hopkins University, where she received the Ernest M. Marks Achievement Award and an AAUW doctoral fellowship to study antibiotic biosynthesis. She began her studies on bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins as an NIH-postdoctoral fellow in microbiology at Harvard Medical School, and during her first tenured faculty appointment in biochemistry at Wright State University School of Medicine.   Wilson's current research focuses on the host-microbe interface; bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins; development of anti-toxin and toxin-based biologics; and comparative and functional genomic technologies and applications involving microbiomes in health and disease.

973.summary: Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne
973.description: It has been more than 30 years since the celebrated violinist Midori graced the stage of the Foellinger Great Hall. Midori, once a child prodigy, is now a violin superstar recognized as a visionary educator and humanitarian whose multiple nonprofit organizations bring music to children and underserved communities. The United Nations appointed Midori a Messenger of Peace in 2007; she was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2021. “In her hands,” said Roberto Prosseda when conferring the 2025 Cremona Musica Award, “the violin is not only an instrument—it becomes a voice for humanity itself.” Midori has enjoyed a longstanding partnership with the Festival Strings Lucerne, a brilliant European chamber ensemble under the leadership of Daniel Dodds. This concert features two works by Beethoven: Egmont, Overture and Symphony No. 2 in D major, op. 36, as well as Violin concerto in D major, op. 35 by Tchaikovsky, and works by Maurice Ravel and Helena Winkelman, both of which pay homage to Haydn. Learn more about Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne

974.description: “Theatre is a doorway,” says illusionist Scott Silven. “A place where we gather in the dark, drawn together by stories that remind us who we are, who we were, and who we might become. It’s where we witness the impossible, feel the weight of the past, and step into the unknown, together. And The Lost Things is about that unknown.” A joyful exploration of wonder, memory, and shared experience, Silven’s awe-inspiring 75-minute show reveals the mysterious side of human nature through breathtaking illusions and an evocative narrative. Directed by Graham McLaren and designed by Jamie Vartan, The Lost Things reminds you that even in loss, there is beauty to be found—and that sometimes, getting lost is the first step toward truly finding yourself. Suitable for ages 12 and up. Krannert Center is a proud co-commissioner of The Lost Things Learn more about Scott Silven's The Lost Things

993.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, February 25th we will hear from Thais Duarte Zappelini, Post Doc with the Brasillinois Initiative at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Transnational Feminisms, Democracy, and Gender Justice in Brazil: Legacies and Challenges of the 1988 Constitution\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  During Brazil’s 1987 Constituent Assembly debates, congresswoman Rose de Freitas declared: “Women demand compliance with the Charter of Rights that the country signed with the United Nations. Either Brazil honors this commitment or withdraws and breaks ties with the United Nations.” Her statement reflected a broader feminist strategy that linked domestic constitutional reform to international human rights commitments. Freitas was one of only 26 women elected to the National Constituent Assembly and had recently returned from the Moscow Conference, which brought together more than 2,300 Latin American women to discuss shared legal and social struggles. Rather than aligning strictly with party agendas, Brazilian women parliamentarians formed the Lipstick Lobby, a cross-party coalition that prioritized gender equality. Their activism contributed to the inclusion of gender-sensitive provisions in the 1988 Constitution and unfolded within a broader context of global feminist mobilization shaped by the United Nations Decade for Women (1975 1985) and the rise of transnational feminist mobilization in Latin America during the 1970s and 1980s.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

997.summary: Up Against Erasure | “Mitsuki: the In-Between” Film Screening and Discussion
997.description: “Mitsuki: The-In Between” is a documentary that follows Mitsuki, a woman of Japanese and Korean descent, as she embarks on a deeply personal journey to uncover the forgotten history of the Jeju April 3rd Massacre—one of Korea’s most tragic and silenced events. Caught between cultures, languages, and generations, Mitsuki navigates the emotional and historical in-between, tracing the scars of her family's past and the legacy of unresolved trauma. Her search becomes a quiet but powerful act of remembrance, bridging identity and memory, silence and truth.  After the screening, respondents Roderick Wilson (East Asian Languages and Cultures and History) and Anna Jungeun Lee (East Asian Languages and Cultures) will discuss the film in the context of the “Up Against Erasure” theme and then open up for audience questions. Film runtime: 47 minutes Directed by Ho-Geun Yang Produced by KBS Cosponsored by the Asian American Cultural Center, the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies, Department of East Asian Languages & Cultures, and the Spurlock Museum of World Cultures.
997.location: Spurlock Museum, Knight Auditorium (600 S Gregory St, Urbana, IL 61801)

1003.summary: Routes, Encounters, Destinations in Medieval Asia (ca. 500–1500)
1003.description: This conference, organized by Gian Piero Persiani (EALC) and Adam Newman (Religion), will bring together scholars working across disciplines to explore how movement, exchange, and place-making shaped the medieval Asian world. Throughout history, people, objects, and knowledge have been on the move, crossing borders, merging in unexpected ways, and continually reshaping cultural and political landscapes. Movement, however, is never abstract—it unfolds through and between places both real and imagined: between origins and destinations, in cities and across frontiers, and along seas, rivers, deserts, and pilgrimage routes. Movement and destination thus exist in a dynamic and dialogical relationship, each defining and transforming the other. This conference examines these entwined histories of mobility and emplacement in Medieval South, Central, and East Asia between 500 and 1500 CE. Participants will approach the topic from diverse methodological and theoretical perspectives, exploring how travel, exchange, and encounter produced religious missions and pilgrimages; facilitated the transmission, translation, and localization of texts and ideas; fostered multilingualism and intertextuality; and animated networks of trade and diplomacy. Equally important will be attention to the physical and imagined sites that anchored these processes—urban centers, frontier zones, ports of exchange, sacred landscapes, and celebrated sites of natural beauty.  Proposed themes include:Pilgrimage and sacred geographies: routes, shrines, and travelers.Routes and networks of knowledge: monastic and scholarly communities, texts, and maps.Cityscapes and landscapes: ports, borderlands, and scenic sites.Multilingualism and translation: linguistic crossings and literary exchange.Trade, objects, and material culture: movement of commodities and artistic forms.

1027.description: KODO is an internationally renowned ensemble dedicated to exploring the limitless rhythmic possibilities of traditional Japanese taiko drumming. The name “KODO” evokes both the “heartbeat,” the primal source of rhythm, and “children of the drum,” reflecting the group’s spirit of vitality and curiosity. Since debuting in 1981, KODO has performed over 7,500 times across more than 50 countries, focusing on cultural connection and human unity. Based on Sado Island off the northwest coast of Japan, KODO blends three core elements in performance: reimagined folk traditions, works by leading composers, and original creations shaped by global influences. Their newest production, Luminance, offers a striking view of KODO’s ever-evolving artistry—fusing powerful taiko with refined theatricality, dynamic choreography, and moments of shimmering stillness. The result is an immersive concert experience that pulses with energy, precision, and a radiant sense of shared human rhythm. Learn more about KODO presents LUMINANCE

1038.description: Oscar-nominated filmmaker Sam Green collaborates with National Book Critics Awardee and environmentalist Rebecca Solnit for the latest of his “live cinema” experiences. In Green’s work, documentary film meets live original music with Green’s own live narration. It’s “a singular experience, and a collective one, with the potential for human connection and human errors” notes The New York Times. Trees is a profoundly moving study of humankind’s relationship to our earthly cohabitants, the silent witnesses to all of humanity across countless events and generations, putting humanity’s place into perspective. Directed and performed by Sam Green with cinematography by Yoni Brook, and featuring actress Judi Dench, poet laureate Ada Limón, scientists, and stories from around the world, Trees marks Green’s most ambitious film yet. Trees is produced by ArKtype and Josh Penn and supported in part by the National Endowment for the Arts. Commissioning partners: The Boston Symphony Orchestra; New World Symphony; Oregon Symphony Orchestra; Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Wiener Festwochen; Barbican Centre; Holland Festival; Stanford Live @ Stanford University; Duke Arts @ Duke University, Durham, NC; The Arts Center at NYU Abu Dhabi; Green Music Center of Sonoma State University; and Arizona Arts Live at University of Arizona Learn more about Sam Green presents Trees

1041.summary: Patricia Owens Book Talk \"Erased: A History of International Thought Without Men\"
1041.description: Patricia Owens Book Talk: Erased: A History of International Thought Without Men. How did women help create the study of international relations, and why were they subsequently written out of its history? Drawing on her book Erased, Patricia Owens explores the ideas, lives, and work of women who shaped the field in twentieth-century Britain. Moving between universities and other centers of intellectual and political life, she examines how gender, race, and institutional power shaped both the production of knowledge and the histories later told about it. The talk considers what recovering these women’s contributions reveals about intellectual erasure and the possibilities for rethinking the history of international thought. Patricia Owens FBA FRHistS is a professor of international relations at the University of Oxford and currently a Leverhulme Major Research Fellow, 2026–29.
