1045.summary: 2027 Gryphon Lecture: School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas
1045.description: Jonna Perrillo, education historian and professor of English education at the University of Texas at El Paso, will deliver the 2027 Gryphon Lecture hosted by the Center for Children's Books in the School of Information Sciences. She will present \"School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas.\" Bio: Jonna Perrillo's scholarship focuses on humanities education and social citizenship formation, both historically and in contemporary schools. She is the author of three books: Uncivil Rights: Teachers, Unions, and the Battle for School Equity (winner of the New Scholar Book Award from the American Education Research Association, 2013) and Educating the Enemy: Teaching Nazis and Mexicans in the Cold War Borderlands (winner of the Southwest Book Award from the Border Regional Library Association, 2023, and the Bolton-Cutter Prize from the Western History Association, 2022, and Uncensored: Educators Speak Out on Teaching in the Time of Book Bans (Harvard Education Press, 2026). Her writing and research have been featured in The New York Times, The Washington Post, TIME magazine, the Boston Review, Education Week, Slate, Post45, The 74 and on PBS and National Public Radio. With Dr. Andrew Newman, she is the three-time co-director of the National Endowment for the Humanities Summer Institute for Teachers, “Making the Good Reader and Citizen: The History of Literature Instruction in American Schools.” In June 2026, she and Newman co-published the open access report \"Atomized English: Fewer Whole Books, More Isolated Learning Experiences.\"

Violinists Sarah Ying Ma (she/they) and Coco Mi (she/they), violist Jasper de Boor (any pronouns), and cellist Drew Dansby (he/him) took their name from an ancient Greek word meaning “to make,” to create something that has never existed before. 1138.summary: The Poet as Seismograph: Ukrainian and Yiddish Poetry of the 1920s and Beyond  A Conference at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
1138.description: The conference \"The Poet as Seismograph: Ukrainian and Yiddish,” explores the parallels and convergences of Yiddish and Ukrainian poetry of the modernist era and beyond, tracing the interaction between poets and poetry in the two languages. In the first quarter of the twentieth century Kyiv and Kharkiv were major centers of new poetry in both languages. Ukrainian and Yiddish poets of the 1920s and 30s imagined their work as sounding boards and listening devices, sensitive to the reverberations of their era. Their poetry transmitted the political and social changes of their time, the sounds generated by new technologies and the pulse of the urban landscape. In 1924 a group of Kyiv Yiddish writers called their movement “Antenna,” for example. The same motif appears around a hundred years later.  The title work of Ukrainian poet Serhii Zhadan’s 2023 poetry collection Antenna (Antena) speaks of an antenna that both drips with blood but also captures unseen “signals of love from the atmosphere.” Specialists in both Ukrainian and Yiddish trace this theme and more in the conference and the volume to follow. The transnational, comparative, multilingual, and historical perspectives offered by this conference are particularly important in our era of heightened nativism and tunnel vision. The two literatures—Yiddish and Ukrainian—have come to the brink of extinction, and Ukrainian culture and Ukraine are currently under threat, making scholarly attention even more important.

1155.summary: Brown Bag Series- Denial, Deterrence, and Disenchantment: Why Many Never Immigrate
1155.description: This book complements abundant research on immigrants by contributing novel data, knowledge, and theories about those who might have immigrated but did not, despite the benefits of migration to immigrants and migrant-origin and migrant-destination societies. The book examines three mechanisms that reduce immigration: denial of visas, deterrence of many from applying for visas, and ex-immigrants' disenchantment with immigration. Jacob Thomas extends the push-pull model of migration into a push-retain-pull-repel model that better explains why potential immigrants remain ambivalently immobile, providing evidence that retain factors in origin societies and repel factors in destination societies counteract and outweigh the push and pull factors that motivate immigration. Might-have-been-immigrants' narratives reveal an (im)mobility paradox: the factors that facilitate migration—socio-economic resources and social ties—also often impede immigration across different stages of the life course. Finally, examining denial, deterrence, and disenchantment alongside each other stimulates readers to think more globally about inequalities in migratory opportunities by revealing how countless people who never immigrate due to either denial, deterrence, or disenchantment are socio-economically stratified with respect to one another in ways that mirror theories of how immigrants are stratified in destination societies.

1160.summary: Seminar Series - Matt Caplan, Associate Professor, Dept. of Physics, Illinois State University
1160.description: Bio: Dr. Caplan joined ISU in the fall of 2019. His PhD from Indiana University in 2017 won the Dissertation Award in Nuclear Physics from the APS, and prior to joining ISU Dr. Caplan was a CITA National Fellow at the McGill Space Institute.  At ISU, he is the chair of the Twelve Thousand Bombs seminar series on nuclear weapons. Outside academia, he is a writer and scientific consultant for the YouTube channels \"In a Nutshell\" by Kurzgesagt and \"PBS Space Time\" by PBS Digital Studio, with writing credits on nearly 100 videos with combined view counts of a billion.  In 2021, Dr. Caplan was an inaugural Next-Generation Fellow of the Physicists Coalition for Nuclear Threat Reduction. He won a Cottrell Scholar Award in 2023, he is a Kavli Scholar of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB (2022-2024), and he is a co-investigator of the Simons Collaboration on Extreme Electrodynamics of Compact Sources (SCEECS).

1170.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, April 1st we will hear from Maria Alejandra Garcia, Assistant Professor in Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Women, Environment, and Gender Backlash in the Global South\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  Despite decades of investment, gender equality in agricultural and natural resource-dependent contexts in the Global South remains far from realized. While women’s access to services such as extension and finance has improved, severe inequalities persist; women continue to face limited access to land, technologies, and inputs, alongside disproportionately heavy workloads and high rates of violence. Efforts by community-based groups, policy initiatives, and development projects have focused on empowering women to bridge these gaps. However, increasing women’s participation in spaces where they have historically been marginalized can also trigger backlash. Recent studies show that programs promoting women’s decision-making and challenging traditional social expectations can generate gender backlash, manifesting as household conflict, increased workloads, and violence against women. Yet, there remains a critical lack of in-depth research explaining how and why this backlash emerges within agricultural and socio-ecological systems.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

The concert begins with Wagner’s Overture to Rienzi before showcasing Musical America’s Instrumentalist of the Year, violinist Augustin Hadelich, in the cinematic and virtuosic Violin Concerto by Korngold. “The essence of Hadelich’s playing,” wrote Robert Battey in The Washington Post, “is beauty: reveling in the myriad ways of making a phrase come alive on the violin, delivering the musical message with no technical impediments whatsoever, and thereby revealing something from a plane beyond ours.” Learn more about Chicago Symphony Orchestra

1181.description: The symposium will explore the timely field convergence of posthumanism and environmental design, especially with regard to how the posthumanist perspective can challenge, guide and even inspire new ways of thinking about the environment and the life that is dependent on it. This in turn can offer new insights into landscape design and the ways that designers think about animals and plants. Part of the mission of the symposium will be to explore and critique what ensues from this perspective. Several provocative questions follow from this approach:· For whom do we design? How can humans coexist in a world shared with animals? What happens when we conceive of animals and plants as architects? What happens when we conceive of animals and plants as clients? We will engage these and many more queries about the impact of newly emerging understandings of agentic and communicative capabilities beyond the human. The symposium will bring together scholars, artists, design professionals and students to consider how we might actualize the principles of multi-species cohabitation and co-design. Public lectures, participatory events, the showcasing of student design work, and transdisciplinary collaborative discussions will take place.

1205.description: The Slavic Reference Service, in collaboration with the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is pleased to announce the inaugural Balkan Research Forum. This forum aims to spotlight Balkan studies and bring together scholars in all disciplines and at all stages of the research process to discuss the theme “Shifting Borders and Identities in the Balkans.” More than simply lines on a map, borders are fluid entities that can be contested, crossed, and intensely personal – extending beyond geographic spaces to shape language, memory, nationality, and belonging. The Balkans have been profoundly impacted by changing borders and by shifting political, social, and cultural landscapes, as well as global dynamics. From the fall of empires and the redrawing of state boundaries to the emergence of new nations, migration, displacement, and the persistence of cultural communities across borders, the region provides a unique opportunity to explore the intersection of territory and identity.  The inaugural Balkan Research Forum invites proposals examining how changing borders have influenced the ways individuals and communities understand identity, including nationality, ethnicity, language, religion, and memory. We particularly invite proposals that examine broader global dynamics that influence Balkan borders and identities.  We welcome contributions from scholars at all career stages and encourage graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, librarians, and archivists to submit proposals.  Participants are welcome to present in any language, but we ask that an accompanying English translation of any remarks and/or materials be provided.  The inaugural Balkan Research Forum will be held on April 8-9, 2027. Those interested in presenting should submit an abstract by February 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m., CST. Zoom details will be shared the week of the forum.  If you are interested in submitting a proposal, please do so here: 202
1205.location: Online, Zoom, link provided to registered participants

1229.summary: Stanley Clarke & Hiromi along with PUBLIQuartet - A Celebration of the Music of Chick Corea
1229.description: National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master Stanley Clarke joins forces with acclaimed pianist Hiromi—both Grammy Award winners—for a powerful tribute to the late Chick Corea. Blending Corea’s iconic compositions with original works inspired by his legacy, the program celebrates a towering figure whose influence spanned bebop, fusion, and beyond. Clarke, Corea’s longtime collaborator in Return to Forever, and Hiromi—mentored by Corea from a young age—honor a shared musical lineage rooted in innovation and expressive freedom. They are joined by PUBLIQuartet, a Grammy-nominated ensemble praised by The Washington Post and The New Yorker for its bold, genre-defying approach to chamber music. This collaboration offers a dynamic and deeply personal celebration of Corea’s enduring impact on the music of our time. Learn more about Stanley Clarke & Hiromi along with PUBLIQuartet - A Celebration of the Music of Chick Corea

1236.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Grammy-nominated children’s artist Uncle Jumbo layers heartfelt lyrics with high-energy music and interactive dance-alongs that get audiences moving together, inspiring young people to dream big, care for one another, and celebrate what makes them unique. A Texas-born son of a disco and reggae DJ, Uncle Jumbo got his start at age four, playing accordion with touring Zydeco bands on his Aunt Helen’s Louisiana porch. Known for his uplifting spirit and magnetic stage presence, he began creating music for children after the birth of his daughter. Her diagnosis with a rare liver disease, and surgery at only three weeks old, sparked a profound gratitude for life and a mission to help raise generations of positive, loving people as One Big Family. “Imagine that somewhere in the untapped treasures of the late Prince’s legendary vault of music is an album made for kids . . . That’s what Uncle Jumbo sounds like.” (Houston Press) Recommended for grades Pre K – 2 Learn more about School Performance: Uncle Jumbo (KCYS)

1243.description: Layli Long Soldier is the author of the collections We (Graywolf, 2026), and Whereas (Graywolf Press, 2017), which won the National Book Critics Circle award, the 2018 PEN/Jean Stein Book Award, and was a finalist for the National Book Award. She also wrote the chapbook Chromosomory (Q Ave Press, 2010), and her work has been widely anthologized in books like Native Voices (Tupelo Press, 2019) and The Larger Voice (NACF, 2022). On Whereas, poet Dean Rader remarks, “What is especially compelling about Long Soldier is that she not only undermines language, she undermines form as well. Elsewhere, I have written about the importance of ‘compositional resistance’ for Native poets. By this, I refer to how a poet composes her poem, the form it takes, how it looks on the page, how its typography expresses itself. Whereas is a masterful example of compositional resistance.” Her poems and critical work have appeared in POETRY Magazine, The New York Times, American Poet, The American Reader, The Kenyon Review, BOMB, American Indian Journal of Culture and Research, PEN America, and The Brooklyn Rail, among many others. In 2015, Long Soldier was awarded a National Artist Fellowship from the Native Arts and Cultures Foundation and a Lannan Literary Fellowship for Poetry. She was awarded a Whiting Writer’s Award in 2016 and was shortlisted for the Griffin Poetry Prize in 2018. In 2021, she received an Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature and the Michael Murphy Memorial Poetry Prize in the UK. Long Soldier earned a BFA from the Institute of American Indian Arts and an MFA from Bard College. She teaches in the MFA Creative Writing Program at the Institute of American Indian Arts and serves as the 2024-25 Endowed Chair at Texas State University. She resides in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Event cosponsored by the Spurlock Museum of World Cultures.
1243.location: Spurlock Museum, Knight Auditorium (600 S Gregory St, Urbana, IL 61801)

1258.description: Taste Makers: Craft & Credit in the Age of AIApril 17, 2027 | Siebel Center for Design, University of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignWhen anyone can generate a screen, a persona, or a prototype in seconds, making things is no longer the hard part. Knowing what’s good is. As AI takes on more of the effort in design work, a designer's value shifts to taste — the craft, care, and point of view to decide what to build, who it's for, and what's worth putting your name on.Last year, UX Days explored how designers work within systems in flux. This year, we turn to the people shaping what comes out of those systems. Together, we'll ask: What makes great work great, how do we develop the taste to recognize it, and who gets the credit when people and machines make things together?Through keynotes, workshops, and conversations, UX Day 2027 bridges the critical and the practical, inviting students, educators, and professionals to sharpen the taste, craft, and ownership that make design human — no matter what tools help us get there. Currently accepting proposals for breakout sessions and keynote speakers. Find more information here.

1263.description: Sinfonia da Camera concludes its season with a program that explores transformation and renewal through music of extraordinary scope and intensity. David DeBoor Canfield’s Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression opens the concert with a work of solemn reflection and contemporary resonance. Stravinsky’s Firebird follows, illuminating the orchestra with its vivid orchestration and mythic narrative of rebirth. Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, conducted from the piano by Ian Hobson, showcases a bold integration of virtuosity and symphonic structure. The season concludes with Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5, a powerful journey from darkness to affirmation. With its sweeping themes and triumphant conclusion, the symphony offers a fitting culmination to a season defined by expressive depth and artistic ambition. Program: David DeBoor Canfield: Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression Igor Stravinsky: The Firebird Franz Liszt: Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, S.124 Ian Hobson, piano and conductor Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky: Symphony No. 5 in E Minor, Op. 64 Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: Firebird Finale

1267.description: Desde 74 Mentorship | Desde 74 is La Casa’s mentorship initiative, reintroduced in Fall 2024, and rooted in our longstanding commitment to mentorship since our founding in 1974. Desde 74 approaches mentorship through alumni engagement, first-year mentorship, outreach to future Illini, and the empowerment of our upperclassmen to serve as mentors. While the program has evolved over the years—from the Peer Retention Program in the 80s and 90s to the ACE (Advising, Connecting, Empowering) mentorship program—its foundation in mentorship and student empowerment has remained constant, leading us to reimagine mentoring through Desde 74 welcoming our largest matches of mentors & mentees in 2024-2025.
1267.location: La Casa Cultural Latina  1203 W. Nevada Street, Urbana, IL 61801, United States

1268.description: The Jupiter String Quartet chose its name because the planet Jupiter was prominent in the night sky at the time of the quartet’s formation in 2001. A particularly intimate group consisting of violinists Mélanie Clapiès and Meg Freivogel, violist Liz Freivogel (Meg’s older sister), and cellist Daniel McDonough (Meg’s husband, Liz’s brother-in-law), the ensemble's star continues to shine brightly as an important voice in the world of chamber music, exuding an energy that is at once friendly, knowledgeable, and adventurous. This program presents Mozart’s String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, “Dissonance” and Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127, alongside Azerbaijani composer Franghiz Ali-Zadeh’s Oasis (String Quartet No. 4). The evocative 1998 composition captivates with its mixture of sounds and textures, moods and pictures. Program: Mozart: String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, K.465, “Dissonance” Franghiz Ali-Zadeh: “Oasis” (String Quartet No. 4) Beethoven: String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127 Learn more about Jupiter String Quartet

1270.summary: School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)
1270.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. It’s the late 1800s, a time of invention. Trains, steamboats, cameras, even electricity are new at the King’s palace in Honolulu. Eleven-year-old Joseph Kekuku accidentally strikes the strings of his guitar with a bolt from a railroad track and unlocks a brand new sound. Hawaiian music—and the music of America—is never the same. Playwright Moses Goods, one of Hawaiʻi’s most prominent theatre artists, in collaboration with Kealakai Center for Pacific Strings, captures the true story of Joseph Kekuku’s invention of the steel guitar (kīkā kila). The multimedia production features a live Hawaiian slide guitar soundtrack and projections as it celebrates innovation, engineering, and the global exchange of ideas and sound. Rich in history, the play also looks forward and encourages children of today to celebrate their voice, culture, and sense of curiosity. Recommended for grades 2-8 Learn more about School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)

1314.description: Created by sweat variant, the acclaimed partnership between artist and MacArthur Fellow Okwui Okpokwasili and director and designer Peter Born, adaku, part 2: she shivers with it. continues a speculative trilogy exploring one family’s entanglement with the transatlantic slave trade. Set in a near-future United States, part 2 investigates the embodied consequences of this violent rupture and the erasure of ancestral knowledge. When transmissions lead to sudden remembering, what is unleashed in the imagination of a young woman who's been led to believe she has no history worth remembering? What are the multitude of futures she can now imagine? sweat variant’s multidisciplinary approach invites audiences into cycles of ritual and repair. The presentation of adaku, part 2: she shivers with it. by Sweat Variant was made possible by the New England Foundation for the Arts' National Dance Project, with lead funding from the Doris Duke Foundation and the Mellon Foundation. Learn more about sweat variant presents adaku, part 2: she shivers with it.

1329.description: Desde 74 Mentorship | Desde 74 is La Casa’s mentorship initiative, reintroduced in Fall 2024, and rooted in our longstanding commitment to mentorship since our founding in 1974. 1331.description: Experience an unforgettable evening with Audra McDonald. Widely regarded as one of the greatest performers of her generation, McDonald is the only artist to win six Tony Awards across all four acting categories, along with two Grammy Awards, an Emmy, and the National Medal of Arts. In this intimate concert setting, she brings her luminous voice and profound interpretive skill to a richly varied program of Broadway favorites, selections from the Great American Songbook, and more. Backed by her ensemble, McDonald creates a deeply personal connection with audiences, blending technical brilliance with emotional depth and storytelling mastery. Whether on stage or screen, her artistry consistently sets the standard for excellence. This special appearance promises an evening of elegance, warmth, and musical brilliance from a truly iconic performer. Learn more about An Evening with Audra McDonald

1468.description: Many students find taking tests, completing assignments, and/or giving presentations very stressful. At times, this stress can be counterproductive and negatively impact performance. The American Test Anxieties Association estimates that between 16 and 20% of college students have high anxiety when it comes to taking tests or performing well on assignments. Fortunately, there are ways to address anxiety so that you can do your best work. During the academic year, we offer drop-in Test Anxiety Workshops. These workshops are free for students, but space is limited, so we request that you register in advance on our website.

1478.description: Many students are told that perfectionism is a good thing and necessary for success. However, studies show that perfectionistic attitudes can interfere with success. The desire to be perfect can both rob you of a sense of personal satisfaction and cause you to fail to achieve as much as people with more realistic expectations. This two-part program helps students realize when perfectionism is more harmful than good and develop more realistic expectations.    This program is open to all Illinois students—you do not need to be a current client of the Counseling Center to register.

1480.summary: Innovative Teaching to Excel and Advance MedEd (iTEAM)
1480.description: iTEAM is an innovative partnership with the ACGME and is guided by the ACGME Medical Educator Competencies. This academic year program explores essential components for effective teaching in medical education. Nationally recognized presenters, education specialist faculty, and instructional coaches facilitate the experience through a collaborative small-group cohort model. The program blends monthly half-day workshops with asynchronous learning and individualized coaching support. Participants receive observation, feedback, and mentoring to strengthen teaching effectiveness across clinical and educational settings. The series is approved for ACCME continuing education credit. Registration opens each Spring/Summer for the following academic year.

1488.summary: Physics Careers Seminar: \"Crossing Disciplines: What a Physics Degree Can Do in Engineering, Quantum Science, and DOE Labs\"
1488.description: Abstract: Physics training opens more doors than most students realize, and the path through them is rarely a straight line. In this talk I will share my own route: a B.S. in physics, a Ph.D. in electrical engineering focused on microelectronics, a postdoc in medical engineering developing optical imaging methods, and now a principal investigator at Oak Ridge National Laboratory working on quantum sensing. Along the way I worked at two universities (USC and Caltech) and two DOE national laboratories (Los Alamos and Oak Ridge). I will discuss how moving across fields shaped the way I choose problems and build collaborations as a PI, and why a physics foundation can be a real advantage in engineering research. I will compare research and career development in universities and national labs, including funding, team structure, research styles, and day-to-day life, to help students and postdocs decide which environment fits them. I will also introduce career resources from the American Physical Society. I will close with my perspective on how AI is reshaping academic research, the opportunities it creates for early-career scientists, and the risks worth watching. Students and postdocs at all stages are welcome. Biography: Dr. Huan Zhao is a Eugene Wigner Distinguished Staff Fellow at the Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences, Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), where he conducts interdisciplinary research in spin-based quantum sensing, solid-state quantum light sources, nanomaterials, optical imaging, and nanoelectronics. He received his B.S. in physics from China, and his Ph.D. in electrical engineering from the University of Southern California in December 2019. From 2019 to 2022, he was a Director’s Postdoctoral Fellow at the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies at Los Alamos National Laboratory. He then joined the Department of Medical Engineering at Caltech as a postdoctoral scholar, working on ultrafast optical imaging, before joining ORNL in December 2023. H

1511.description: The campus seeks to nominate sophomores and juniors for the prestigious Udall Scholarship. The Udall awards $7,000 to sophomores or juniors who are taking action to address environmental concerns and are committed to a career related to the environment. Students must be US citizens, US nationals, or US permanent residents. A successful applicant will have a GPA of 3.0 or higher and demonstrate leadership and a commitment to service. The University of Illinois may nominate up to six students for the Udall Scholarship. The campus deadline is January 25, 2027 to be considered. If you are interested in applying, please plan to attend our Udall sessions.  On Thursday December 3, 2026 from 3:30pm - 4:30pm there will be an information session and discussion with a former Udall Scholar and on Friday December 4, 2026 from 3:00pm - 4:00pm is a workshop on how to craft a Udall Application.  These sessions are being held in 514 IUB.Please note that there are also Udall awards for Native American students interested in tribal policy or health care (no need to be related to the environment).* For more information, contact the scholarships office at topscholars@illinois.edu or visit our website at Udall – National & International Scholarships Program
1511.location: Illini Union Bookstore Building, fifth floor #514, 807 S Wright St Champaign IL, 61820

1512.description: Many students find taking tests, completing assignments, and/or giving presentations very stressful. At times, this stress can be counterproductive and negatively impact performance. The American Test Anxieties Association estimates that between 16 and 20% of college students have high anxiety when it comes to taking tests or performing well on assignments. Fortunately, there are ways to address anxiety so that you can do your best work. During the academic year, we offer drop-in Test Anxiety Workshops. These workshops are free for students, but space is limited, so we request that you register in advance on our website.

1523.description: Join us to learn about this unique opportunity for intellectual and professional development at esteemed UK universities! The US-UK Fulbright Commission offers special Summer Institutes for US citizens to study in the UK. These summer programs provide the opportunity for undergraduates (aged over 18), with at least two years of undergraduate study left to complete, to go to the UK on a three, four, five, or six week academic and cultural summer program.  The Summer Institutes cover the majority of the participant costs (round-trip airfare from the US to the UK, tuition and fees at the university, room and board, and social programs).  More information about the institutes and their application can be found at: UK Summer Institutes | Fulbright . Our info session will highlight the benefits of attending a UK Fulbright Summer Institute and how to be a competitive applicant. We hope to see you there!
1523.location: Illini Union Bookstore Building, fifth floor #514, 807 S Wright St Champaign IL, 61820

1525.summary: Innovative Teaching to Excel and Advance MedEd (iTEAM)
1525.description: iTEAM is an innovative partnership with the ACGME and is guided by the ACGME Medical Educator Competencies. This academic year program explores essential components for effective teaching in medical education. Nationally recognized presenters, education specialist faculty, and instructional coaches facilitate the experience through a collaborative small-group cohort model. The program blends monthly half-day workshops with asynchronous learning and individualized coaching support. Participants receive observation, feedback, and mentoring to strengthen teaching effectiveness across clinical and educational settings. The series is approved for ACCME continuing education credit. Registration opens each Spring/Summer for the following academic year.

1540.description: If you are a high-achieving junior and are planning to attend graduate school after graduation, but have concerns about being able to afford it, consider applying for the Beinecke Scholarship. The National and International Scholarships Program has planned sessions to assist students towards earning this $35,000 award. January 28, 2027 we will be conducting an informational session, including a question and answer period with a previous recipient, from 3:30pm - 4:30pm and on January 29, 2027 a Beinecke workshop from 3:00pm - 4:00pm to help students get started on applications.  Both sessions will be held in 514 IUB.The Beinecke Foundation is looking for students who have demonstrated superior standards of intellectual ability, scholastic achievement, and personal promise during their undergraduate years. The program seeks to encourage and enable highly motivated U.S. citizen juniors to pursue graduate studies in the arts, humanities, and social sciences. Each scholar receives $5,000 immediately prior to entering graduate school and an additional $30,000 while attending graduate school. Preference is given to candidates for whom the awarding of significant financial aid would increase the likelihood of the student's being able to attend graduate school. For more information, contact the scholarships office at topscholars@illinois.edu or visit our website at Beinecke – National & International Scholarships Program

1588.description: ACGME – CIMED (C.O.M.P.A.S.S. PROGRAM) Assessment is essential to all levels of education, and UME and GME are no exception. With the introduction of competency and outcome-based education, and with the ACGME’s current accreditation model that includes the Milestones, the urgency for high-quality Medical Education programs to meet the needs of learners and the public has grown substantially. The program goal for C.O.M.P.A.S.S. is to enhance the assessment competencies of undergraduate and graduate medical education faculty by providing a comprehensive, experiential learning experience that equips participants with advanced skills in competency-based medical education, assessment methodology, and learner evaluation strategies. The key topics highlight:  – Competency-Based Medical Education principles – Outcome-focused assessment methods – Milestones and EPAs implementation – Practical application of assessment tools – Assessment systems development – Skills enhancement for UME and GME faculty – Strategies for effective learner evaluation Our target audience includes all UME and GME faculty, including residency and fellowship program directors, associate program directors, chairs, members of Clinical Competency Committees (CCCs), and any faculty members with major responsibility for the assessment of learners. Registration opens February 2027.

1600.summary: Crisis by Design: Emergency Powers and Colonial Legality in Puerto Rico
1600.description: Join us for a talk by Jose Atiles, associate professor in the Department of Sociology, about his book, \"Crisis by Design: Emergency Powers and Colonial Legality in Puerto Rico.\"Crisis by Design offers an interdisciplinary sociolegal analysis of the role of law, emergency powers, and anticorruption mobilizations in Puerto Rico’s ongoing multilayered crisis. From the 2006 public debt crisis and the government’s bankruptcy in 2016 to the devastation of Hurricanes Irma, María, and Fiona, the 2020 earthquakes, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the anticorruption uprisings of 2019, Puerto Rico’s recent history has been shaped by overlapping crises that have deepened inequality and citizen vulnerability. Rather than viewing these crises as isolated events, this talk argues that they are integral to the legal structure of colonialism, which actively produces and sustains disaster conditions.Drawing on eight years of qualitative research—including ethnography, semi-structured interviews, archival analysis, and policy review—Crisis by Design examines the legal and political mechanisms that manufacture and manage crisis in Puerto Rico. The book introduces three key concepts: the colonial state of exception, which frames US colonialism as a permanent legal structure of inclusion/exclusion; colonial legality, which captures the legal practices, policies, and economic frameworks sustaining Puerto Rico’s crisis management; and legal interruptions, which describes civil society efforts to mobilize transparency laws and accountability measures as a form of resistance. These mobilizations, together with grassroots demonstrations, or what I term colonial ruptures, challenge the repetitive temporality of colonial legality, underscoring a radical possibility for rendering the colonial legal structure in Puerto Rico ineffective.By critically engaging with law, power, and resistance in Puerto Rico, Crisis by Design contributes to global debates on colonialism, legal governance, and crisis mana

1603.summary: Info session: AGCM 398 - Rhetoric of Wine and Cheese - France
1603.description: Learn more about AGCM 398 - Rhetoric of Wine and Cheese in France! This program is open to all majors. Pizza will be provided while supplies last! Language drives our understanding of food, and especially wine. The words and images we use to describe their taste, origin, and production, and desirability are communications choices. In this course, we will study how discourse and images construct national identities, social status, cultural narratives, and an ethos of sustainability. We pay special attention to the culture of France, considering the ways that land and location are central organizing concepts, especially through the concepts of terroir and appellations.

1629.summary: High School and Community College Student Open House and Portfolio Review
1629.description: Our Regional High School and Community College Portfolio Day provides an excellent opportunity for your students to learn about the opportunities available at our institution and to receive valuable feedback on their current work. Faculty and staff members from the School’s recruitment committee will provide portfolio reviews, answer program-specific questions, and offer general guidance on the application process for first-year and community college transfer students. Faculty insights and guidance can significantly impact your students' futures. This event will also showcase the exceptional visual and scholarly works created by our current undergraduate cohort in the Studio Art, Graphic Design, Industrial Design, Art and Art History, and Art Education programs. Student ambassadors will lead tours of our outstanding facilities as well as answering questions about our programs and campus life. Light refreshments will be offered in our Link Galley location. Even better, this year the open house coincides with our Art & Design Fall Fest event, a day of undergraduate arts celebration, featuring open classrooms, workshops and demos. We’d love to have you here to experience this annual event. To be prepared for a portfolio review, students should ideally bring their original works of art in a portfolio. Large scale, video, or 3D works can be presented digitally, and laptops and tablets are great options. 10-20 artworks completed within the last two years, including works in drawing, painting, textiles, collage, illustration, photography, two and three-dimensional design, ceramics, sculpture, and printmaking are encouraged. Sketchbooks can also provide valuable insights into the creative planning and thinking process and we encourage you to bring those along, as well.  The School of Art & Design is an original charter member of the National Association of Schools of Art and Design (NASAD), and we’ve maintained our fully accredited status for over 75 years. 2020.summary: Why We Need Another Book About Wool | Book Launch and Talk
2020.description: Join us for the book launch and talk on Melisa Littlefield's new book, Reinventing Wool: How a Natural Fiber Survived the Synthetic Revolution (Johns Hopkins University Press)Most of us have read a book about sheep or wool: Clara Parkes, Brett Bannor, and Peggy Hart are just a few of the authors who have given us new perspectives on the natural fiber. So why do we need another book about wool? In the guild's November program, Melisa Littlefield will explore some of her latest research about wool in the mid-20th century. She'll share some of the interesting documents, stories, and people that changed the course of wool's trajectory. And she'll offer some thoughts about wool's possible futures. There will be plenty of time for questions! Copies of Melissa's book, Reinventing Wool: How a Natural Fiber Survived the Synthetic Revolution, will be available for purchase. Reinventing Wool Book Summary (short version) Wool once shaped daily life in the United States. The textile clothed soldiers and filled civilian wardrobes; sheep even grazed on the White House lawn. Today, however, wool apparel represents a sliver of the global textile market. In Reinventing Wool, Melissa M. Littlefield uncovers the surprising story behind this dramatic shift. Weaving together textile science, advertising archives, governmental reports, and her own experience as a fiber artist, Littlefield highlights the cultural forces that reshaped wool's reputation.
2020.location: The Good Shepherd Lutheran Church, 2101 S Prospect Ave, Champaign

2021.summary: Cancer Engineering & Biology Program Fall Showcase
2021.description: About the Showcase The Cancer Engineering & Biology (CEB) Program showcase will bring together CEB faculty, trainees, and working groups to connect and share research. The program will feature scientific talks, working group updates, a keynote presentation, and a poster session showcasing trainee research.  Keynote Speaker Kay F. Macleod Hospira Foundation Professor of Oncology  Professor, Ben May Department for Cancer Research, The University of Chicago  Associate Director, Basic Sciences, University of Chicago Comprehensive Cancer Center  Talk: ATF4 is required for KRas-driven pancreatic tumorigenesis to suppress early-stage p53 induction Macleod focuses on understanding the role of mitophagy in mitochondrial stress responses and cancer cell signaling, and explores the significance of mitochondrial dysfunction in cancer etiology and treatment. Learn more about Macleod's research here.

2024.summary: IQUIST Young Researchers Seminar: \"Signatures of Quantum Phase Structure and Criticality in Restricted Boltzmann Machine Neural Quantum States,\" Javier Montaner, Clark Group
2024.description: \"Signatures of Quantum Phase Structure and Criticality in Restricted Boltzmann Machine Neural Quantum States\"Abstract: Neural network quantum state tomography (NNQST) can reconstruct quantum states with fewer samples than conventional tomography. However, the utilized neural network is viewed as a black box. In this work we try to look inside by training restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) on measurement data from the ground state of the one-dimensional transverse field Ising model (TFIM) and analyzing the singular value decomposition of the fully-trained weight matrix. We find that the learned internal structure of the RBM reflects the physics of the system it represents. The spectrum of singular values is different for each phase of the TFIM, in accordance with the different measurement distributions in each phase. We also see unique behavior in the model trained at the critical point. Here the singular values decay exponentially but also the singular vectors form clear sinusoids which appear to coincide with the eigenfunctions of an equivalent system, the particle in a box. Our results hold independent of system size, indicating they are universal properties of learned models. In addition we note the dependence of this analysis on the sample complexity and size of the latent space as well as a discussion of the RBM's training dynamics where we find further evidence of a series of symmetry-breaking transitions. Bio: Javier is a 5th year grad student working with Bryan Clark on machine learning applications in physics. 2025.summary: The Anthony J Leggett Institute for Condensed Matter Special Theory Seminar, Shivaji Sondhi (Oxford), \"How might quantum platforms reshape many-body physics?\"
2025.description: Title: How might quantum platforms reshape many-body physics? Abstract: Quantum platforms are nearing a scale where they will allow the realization of a vast number of quantum circuits. Some of these will solve computational problems of interest to industry and commerce, others will answer questions about quantum systems that we normally ask. But this will still leave much room for searching for entirely new quantum phenomena. In this talk I will describe some thinking on how we might do this and what we might search for. The basic idea will be that these quantum devices will be in constant dialog with classical computers. It is simplest to imagine that a single classical computer will seek to maximize an \"interest function\" which captures the novelty of the circuit. More generally multiple classical computers may search for a Nash equilibrium involving their separate measures of interest. One can think of this mode of joint optimization as constituting a third \"discovery mode\" use of the device apart from simulation and computation modes.  Zoom Link: https://illinois.zoom.us/my/icmt.seminar?pwd=ZU1KbnBLeXZLUmJKc0oyU205cDNDdz09 Meeting ID: 791 382 8328 Password: 106237

2027.description: Sonogenetic Engineering of Programmable Cell and Gene Therapies Abstract: How can we engineer cells to “hear” sound waves and translate them into precise therapeutic responses? Dr. Longwei Liu’s research integrates sonogenetic engineering, synthetic biology, and molecular imaging to develop remotely controllable cell and gene therapies. His laboratory uses focused ultrasound (FUS) to achieve spatial and temporal control of therapeutic activity in cancer and inherited retinal diseases. Recent work includes engineering ultrasound-controllable CAR-T cells for solid tumors, including feedback-regulated systems that sustain antitumor activity after transient ultrasound stimulation, and developing FUS-controlled CRISPR and genome-editing platforms for precision gene therapy. His group also develops genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors and multiplexed imaging approaches to visualize intracellular signaling and guide therapeutic circuit design. In this seminar, Dr. Liu will highlight advances in sonogenetic CAR-T therapy, remotely controlled genome engineering, and molecular imaging, illustrating how focused ultrasound can serve as a noninvasive interface for programming therapeutic cells and genes in vivo. Biography: Dr. Longwei Liu is an Assistant Professor of Ophthalmology and Biomedical Engineering at the University of Southern California (USC). He completed his postdoctoral training in Bioengineering at the University of California, San Diego (2019–2022) and received his Ph.D. in Biomedical Engineering from Tsinghua University in 2018. Dr. Liu’s research integrates synthetic biology, focused ultrasound, genome engineering, and molecular imaging to develop remotely controllable cell and gene therapies for cancer and inherited eye diseases. His work focuses on ultrasound-controllable CAR-T cell therapies, sonogenetic regulation of genome and genetically encoded biosensors for investigating cellular signaling.   Dr. Liu has received numerous awards and honors, inclu

2028.description: This talk will consider how Indigenous political and legal thought, story, and material culture challenge the rhetoric and logics of American gun culture.  For centuries, Indigenous people have been on the frontlines of American gun violence and have analyzed the US settler state in terms of its guns. Building upon deep-rooted theories of relationality and human-material interactions, Indigenous understandings of gun violence run much deeper than the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms. Today’s American gun violence is, I argue, directly related to centuries of settler attacks on Indigenous governance and settler erasure of Indigenous thought. More broadly, this talk emphasizes the vital importance of Indigenous writing, philosophy, and archives to understanding America today.

2036.summary: Condensed Matter Journal Club: \"Mapping Altermagnetic Symmetry through Quantum Oscillations in CrSb\"
2036.description: Altermagnets exhibit momentum-dependent spin splitting despite having compensated magnetic order. Establishing the symmetry of this splitting experimentally is essential for understanding their electronic properties. In this journal club, I will discuss recent quantum-oscillation measurements of CrSb that resolve its three-dimensional, g-wave altermagnetic spin texture. By tracking oscillation frequencies as the magnetic field rotates, the study identifies frequency branches that separate away from symmetry-enforced nodal orientations and merge upon approaching them. Comparison with electronic-structure calculations connects this angular evolution to the underlying magnetic symmetry. I will examine the evidence for assigning these branches to spin-split Fermi surfaces, discuss the interpretation’s limitations, and consider how quantum oscillations can probe unconventional magnetic order beyond conventional Fermi-surface characterization.

2040.summary: Instructional Seminar Series, Dr. Kevin Lin, \"Reimagining CS Education: Agentic Engineering, Authentic Assessment, and Human-Centered Design for Learner Agency.\"
2040.description: Abstract: Computers have always been good at giving answers; generative AI makes answers nearly frictionless. For computing education, which has long treated producing code as evidence of learning, this raises a question about what we value and whose judgment we are cultivating. In software engineering, the bottleneck is shifting from writing code toward architecting, specifying, verifying, and taking responsibility for code no one wrote by hand. Yet the curricula, assessments, and professional norms emerging around this shift are being designed largely in and for a narrow slice of the world’s learners and workplaces. Drawing on a synthesis from the Consortium for Generative AI in CS Education and on classroom experiments at the University of Washington, this talk offers five paired frames—questions and answers, past and present, depth and breadth, learner and agent, self and society—for reimagining computing education. Along the way, it considers how students can learn to interrogate the design assumptions built into everyday technologies, how assessment can measure the learner rather than the agent, how “everyone can code” changes who computing education is for, and how community-engaged projects and dialogue can rebuild the agency that frictionless tools can erode. Bio: Kevin Lin (he/him) is an Associate Teaching Professor in the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering at the University of Washington, where he co-directs the Center for Learning, Computing, and Imagination. He leads instructional innovation in data programming and data structures with a focus on empowering students to redesign computing problems and artifacts. Kevin received his MS in Computer Science from UC Berkeley, where he coordinated the teaching and delivery of very large-scale undergraduate CS courses to over 1,000 students per semester.

2043.summary: Machine Learning Seminar: Dr. Lisha Chen, \"Preference-Guided Model Steering to Explore Trade-offs on the Pareto Front.\"
2043.description: Abstract: When a learning system balances competing objectives, such as helpfulness and safety in an LLM, how can it offer trade-offs that reflect users’ preferences? A common approach is to vary the weights assigned to each objective. However, the distribution of objective weights often does not match users’ desired distribution of model performance on the Pareto front (PF). To address this mismatch, I will first introduce SURF, an analytically tractable method for bi-objective problems. It targets settings where users want a diverse menu of trade-offs, ideally uniform on the PF. Our analysis shows that the mismatch arises because, as the objective weight varies, the solutions trace the PF at a non-uniform speed. The arc-length map records the distance traveled along the front as a function of the weight; by estimating and inverting it, SURF selects weights that yield uniformly distributed points on the PF. SURFACE extends this idea to higher-dimensional PFs, general distributions beyond the uniform one, and general scalarization methods. With more than two objectives, arc length generalizes to the area or volume of regions on the PF, and SURFACE generalizes SURF by estimating how regions in weight space map to regions of different volumes on the PF. Finally, I will discuss applications to multi-objective reinforcement learning, LLM alignment, and multi-task speech LLMs, where adjusting objective weights during training or fine-tuning helps steer a model toward users’ preferred trade-offs among objectives or tasks. Bio: Lisha Chen is an Assistant Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Rochester. Her research spans machine learning, optimization, and statistical signal and image processing, with a current focus on multi-objective and multi-level optimization and learning. She earned her Ph.D. and M.S. from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and her B.S. from Huazhong University of Science and Technology. She has delivered tutorials at IC

2044.description: Title: A new large sieve method in combinatorics Abstract: We discuss a new method of converting local congruence restrictions into global information, based on the Chinese remainder theorem. 2046.summary: Book Launch: A Queer Genealogy of US Citizenship, Race, and Sexuality by Siobhan Somerville
2046.description: Please join us for a Book Launch followed by a reception and book-signingto celebrate the publication of: Naturalization: A Queer Genealogy of US Citizenship, Race, and Sexuality (Duke University Press) by Siobhan Somerville All are welcome!Books will be available for purchase courtesy of the Illini Union Bookstore. About the author: Siobhan B. Somerville is Associate Professor of English and Gender and Women’s Studies at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. She is the author of Queering the Color Line: Race and the Invention of Homosexuality in American Culture, also published by Duke University Press, and the editor of The Cambridge Companion to Queer Studies.  About the book (Introduction available here) Amid contentious debates about citizenship, borders, and belonging, naturalization tends to stand apart, widely celebrated as the culmination of immigrant narratives and American ideals of liberalism. In Naturalization, Siobhan B. Somerville unsettles this story, showing how the process of citizen-making has historically been embedded in normative assumptions about race, indigeneity, and sexuality that have sustained the US settler colonial project. Tracing an alternative genealogy of naturalization from the eighteenth century through the mid-twentieth, Somerville investigates overlooked stories not only of immigrants but also of Indigenous people, formerly enslaved people of African descent, and inhabitants of US territories, many of whom became US citizens through collective naturalization, often without their consent. Somerville’s interdisciplinary approach to a wide-ranging archive—including federal law, photographs, letters, and memoirs—shows how naturalization has long functioned as both a powerful metaphor and a contradictory material practice at the core of the US settler colonial state.

2047.description: Title: The \theta=\infty Conjecture and the Riemann Hypothesis Abstract: The Riemann Hypothesis is closely connected to the behavior of moments of the Riemann zeta function. In particular, a conjecture of Bettin and Gonek asserts that suitably normalized mollified second moments remain bounded even when the mollifier has arbitrarily large polynomial length. This is known as the \theta=\infty conjecture. In this talk, we will discuss an extension of this conjecture to automorphic L-functions and its consequences for the distribution of their zeros. We will see how bounds for mollified moments imply zero-free regions and how an averaged version of the conjecture leads to a quasi-Riemann Hypothesis for families of automorphic L-functions.

2055.summary: IQUIST Seminar: \"Scanning NV Microscopy for Quantum Materials: From Magnetic Imaging to Nanoscale EPR\", Huan Zhao, Eugene Wigner Distinguished Staff Fellow, Oak Ridge National Laboratory
2055.description: \"Scanning NV Microscopy for Quantum Materials: From Magnetic Imaging to Nanoscale EPR\" Abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond provide a powerful platform for nanoscale magnetic sensing, combining high spatial resolution with broad experimental compatibility. In this talk, I will briefly introduce the principles of scanning NV microscopy and then focus on two recent applications to quantum materials and spin systems. First, I will discuss scanning NV magnetometry using altermagnetic α-MnTe as an example, where nanoscale magnetic imaging reveals domain structures and their evolution under applied strain. I will then show how scanning NV relaxometry can be extended to nanoscale electron paramagnetic resonance (nano-EPR). Using spin defects in hexagonal boron nitride as a model system, cross-relaxation between the NV sensor and target spins enables local ESR spectroscopy and spatial mapping of spin-defect density without requiring direct optical readout of the target spins. I will conclude with ongoing work using quantum-logic-assisted repetitive readout to improve the sensitivity and imaging speed of scanning NV relaxometry. All work was conducted at the Center for Nanophase Materials Sciences (CNMS), a U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science user facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. I will also briefly introduce CNMS capabilities and the process for submitting a user proposal. Bio: Dr. Huan Zhao is a research scientist at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), where he conducts interdisciplinary research in spin-based quantum sensing, solid-state quantum light sources, nanomaterials, optical imaging, and nanoelectronics. He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering from the University of Southern California in December 2019. From 2019 to 2022, he was a Director’s Postdoctoral Fellow at the Center for Integrated Nanotechnologies at Los Alamos National Laboratory. He subsequently joined the Department of Medical Engineering at Caltech as a postdo

2058.description: Title: Ramsey numbers of loose triangles versus cliquesAbstract: An $r$-uniform loose triangle $C_3$ consists of three edges that pairwise intersect in distinct single vertices. The Ramsey number $R(C_3,K_t^{(r)})$ is a natural hypergraph analogue of the classical graph Ramsey number $R(3,t)=\Theta(t^2/\log t)$. Motivated by the logarithmic saving in the graph case, Kostochka, Mubayi, and Verstra\\"ete conjectured in 2013 that $R(C_3,K_t^{(r)})=o(t^{3/2})$ for every fixed $r\ge3$. We resolve this conjecture by proving that $R(C_3,K_t^{(r)})=O_r\big(t^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log\log t}\big)$. This is joint work with Ayush Basu and Abhishek Dhawan.

2061.summary: Alumnus DAIS Seminar: Prof. Yu Meng, \"Beyond Brute-Force Compute: Training Light and Thinking Deep for LLM Reasoning.\"
2061.description: Abstract: Large language models have made remarkable progress on challenging reasoning tasks by scaling computation at both training and inference time. However, more compute does not automatically mean better reasoning: Reinforcement learning can over-reinforce behaviors the model already favors, extended training yields diminishing returns, and longer reasoning traces can reflect overthinking. In this talk, I will explore how understanding the structure of LLM reasoning lets us use computation more efficiently.First, I will examine what reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) actually teaches: penalizing incorrect responses alone is surprisingly effective, often matching or surpassing PPO and GRPO across the Pass@k spectrum while preserving diversity. Second, I will show that RLVR weight updates are dominated by a single rank-1 direction whose magnitude grows nearly linearly, allowing us to extrapolate checkpoints that match or approach full RLVR from only the first 15–20% of training. Finally, I will introduce an efficient inference-time scaling method by identifying deep-thinking tokens, whose predictions keep being revised in later layers and reflect more thinking efforts. Their proportion tracks accuracy more reliably than output length, and selecting samples by it matches self-consistency at roughly half the inference cost.Together, these results show that efficient reasoning comes not from more computation, but from understanding what RL learns, exploiting the structure of training dynamics, and spending inference compute where it matters.Short Bio: Yu Meng is an assistant professor of the Computer Science Department at the University of Virginia. His research focuses on developing more capable, efficient, and aligned Large Language Models (LLMs). 2066.summary: IQUIST Young Researchers Seminar: \"Exact unitary designs under symmetry,\" Chris Vairogs, Leditzky Group
2066.description: \"Exact unitary designs under symmetry\"Abstract: Unitary designs are ensembles of unitary operators that mimic the statistical properties of the uniformly random Haar measure over the unitary group. They have emerged as a key tool in various randomized techniques within modern quantum information science. Simultaneously, symmetries impose constraints on the implementable unitary operations in a physical setting. This limitation motivates the introduction of a symmetric unitary t-design as an ensemble of operators whose t-th statistical moments match those of the Haar measure over the full group of unitary operators commuting with a given symmetry group. Symmetric t-designs may retain the utility of unitary t-designs for many quantum information processing applications adapted to the symmetry-constrained setting. In this talk, we investigate constructions for symmetric t-designs in the form of sub-ensembles of unitary t-designs for symmetries that reflect physical limitations in quantum devices. The content of this talk is based off of the following paper: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.40227. Bio: Chris Vairogs is a 5th year Physics Ph.D. Student researching unitary randomization and multipartite entanglement under the guidance of his supervisor Felix Leditzky.      IQUIST is committed to providing a safe, inclusive, and respectful environment for all participants at our sponsored events. 2076.summary: Nonlinear viscoelastic friction reduction in the infinite length journal bearing
2076.description: Abstract: Viscoelastic fluids in shear produce normal stresses. These normal stresses have previously been included in the infinite length journal bearing through a linear viscoelastic model that predicts normal stress generation but not shear thinning. Real polymeric solutions (which are used routinely in lubrication applications) exhibit normal stress generation and shear thinning. Therefore, nonlinear viscoelastic models must be considered. Here, nonlinear viscoelasticity is included through using the Criminale-Ericksen-Filbey (CEF) model (which includes shear thinning, normal stress generation, and terminal regime viscoelasticity) in the Cauchy momentum equations in polar coordinates in the thin film limit. The resulting equations are solved using a perturbation expansion that yields a modified Reynolds equation (CEF-Reynolds equation) for the infinite length journal bearing that includes shear thinning, viscoelastic effects, and fluid inertia. The CEF-Reynolds equation matches predictions for purely viscous fluids across all eccentricity ratios, validating the model. This provides a computationally inexpensive method that can be used for designing fluid and bearing performance for decreasing friction in lubricated sliding.  This talk will focus on the mathematical structure and computations used to solve the complex system.  Bio: Dr. Schuh is a Teaching Associate Professor and the Associate Head for MEng Programs in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He received his BS and MS in Mechanical Engineering in 2013 and 2015, his PhD in Theoretical and Applied Mechanics in 2018, and his MBA in 2021, all from the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign. His technical interests include electrical energy storage, tribology, rheology, and computational physics, and his teaching interests include improving learning outcomes in engineering curriculum.

2093.summary: Using AI as a Tool, Not a Shortcut: AI Integration in RST 460's Event Planning Process
2093.description: In RST 460 (Event Management in Recreation, Sport & Tourism), students work with community partners to plan and facilitate events in the community. This fall, students in the Event Management course are using AI tools intentionally throughout their semester-long event planning process. For each component of students’ event plan, they are drafting that section with their group without the use of any technology, use an AI tool for feedback on their draft, critique the AI output for accuracy, bias, and fit with their specific attendees and event, and then revise the section (making specific note of how AI was used in that portion). The goal is not to have AI plan the events, but for students to develop their AI literacy alongside the human-centered creativity and judgment that event professionals need. My aim is to help the students become confident, but not dependent, users of AI in the event planning process. I will share how the assignments in the course are structured and the reasoning behind the design, and will also share some preliminary data about students’ experience with the AI integration into the event planning process: what they are finding useful, confusing, or surprising.

2096.summary: RF Signal Processing in Silicon: From Sub-THz Beamforming to Ultra-Broadband Spectrum Sensing
2096.description: Abstract:The growing demand for ultra-high-data-rate connectivity and high-resolution imaging is pushing wireless technologies into the mmWave and sub-THz spectrum (30–300 GHz). While this spectrum offers unprecedented bandwidth, its practical use is challenged by severe path loss and the limited efficiency of silicon transistors at these frequencies. To overcome these challenges, I will present our recent innovations in RF-domain signal processing in silicon that enable scalable beamforming architectures and energy-efficient processing of extremely wide bandwidths. I first will introduce two key building blocks for scalable sub-THz beamformer arrays: a trombone-inspired sub-THz phase shifter that achieves calibration-free, precise phase control, and an ultra-compact, high-power sub-THz bidirectional transceiver front-end. I will then present an RF-domain signal processor inspired by phased-array principles that enables energy-efficient, ultra-broadband spectrum sensing beyond the limits of conventional digital approaches.

2115.summary: Astrophysics, Relativity, and Cosmology Seminar - Katie Harrington (Argonne National Laboratory) \"The Simons Observatory: Commissioning and Early Observations for the Mid-frequency Small Aperture Telescopes\"
2115.description: The Simons Observatory (SO) is a cosmic microwave background (CMB) survey experiment observing from an altitude of 5,200 m in the Atacama Desert in Chile. The SO Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) will cover six spectral bands between 30 and 280 GHz primarily to search for evidence of primordial gravitational waves in the large angular scale B-modes of the CMB polarization. The first two Mid-Frequency (MF) SATs, operating in the 90 and 150 GHz frequency bands, began commissioning observations in late 2023. I will discuss the telescope designs, commissioning observations and results, and analysis from our initial science observations.

2116.summary: CWS: Dr. Angela Calcaterra, \"Rewriting the Story of American Gun Violence\"
2116.description: This talk will consider how Indigenous political and legal thought, story, and material culture challenge the rhetoric and logics of American gun culture.  For centuries, Indigenous people have been on the frontlines of American gun violence and have analyzed the US settler state in terms of its guns. Building upon deep-rooted theories of relationality and human-material interactions, Indigenous understandings of gun violence run much deeper than the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms. Today’s American gun violence is, I argue, directly related to centuries of settler attacks on Indigenous governance and settler erasure of Indigenous thought. 2141.summary: The Physics Colloquium: Dylan Yost (Colorado State University) \"Precision tests of quantum electrodynamics through hydrogen spectroscopy and vacuum birefringence\"
2141.description: Quantum electrodynamics (QED) is the most highly tested theory in science, with predictions made and experimentally confirmed at the parts-per-trillion level.  Because of this extremely accurate theory, testing QED predictions with increased precision can provide more accurate determinations of fundamental constants or reveal deviations that indicate new physics.  In this talk, I will discuss our lab’s efforts to test QED predictions through two avenues.  The first is our ongoing effort in precision hydrogen spectroscopy where we recently measured narrow 2S-nS two-photon transitions. The second is a new experimental effort where we will attempt to detect photon-photon interaction using femtosecond lasers coupled to high finesse optical cavities.

2149.summary: Condensed Matter Seminar - \"The tenfold way on a finite Hilbert space: topology of entanglement for qubits and fermions\"
2149.description: The tenfold classification of topological matter applies equally to finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, where it classifies the generators of entanglement. For two qubits, time-reversal-symmetric Hamiltonians split into five disconnected phases (ℤ₅), with Bell states as zero-dimensional edge states; for two fermions in graphene vacancy modes, particle–hole symmetry plays the same role and adds orbital entanglement with no qubit analog. A sum rule relates the winding number of any gate to measurable Berry phases. Topology is necessary, but not sufficient, for entanglement.

2157.summary: The Physics Colloquium: Ahmet Yildiz (University of California Berkeley) \"Stepping dynamics of dynein characterized by MINFLUX\"
2157.description: Dynein is the primary motor responsible for nearly all motility and force generation towards the minus ends of microtubules (MTs) in cells. The dynamics of dynein stepping have been poorly characterized by tracking flexible regions at limited resolution. We developed a cysteine-light mutant of dynein and site-specifically labeled its MT-binding domain.  MINFLUX tracking at sub-millisecond resolution revealed that dynein hydrolyzes one ATP per step and takes multitudes of 8 nm steps. The stepping monomer takes backward “dips” due to MT release and subsequent diffusion around the MT-bound partner before a minus-end-directed conformational change of its linker. Our results reveal the order of events that result in a productive step of dynein.

2163.summary: Condensed Matter Seminar - \"Nonconventional magnets: from materials to devices\"
2163.description: Nonconventional magnets are a class of magnetic materials that combine aspects of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, possessing zero net magnetization like antiferromagnets but exhibiting (potentially large) spin splitting of the electronic bands and anomalous Hall responses like ferromagnets. Recent research has focused on magnetic systems with odd-parity spin splitting of nonrelativistic origin (p-wave magnets), which are promising for spintronic applications. Symmetry considerations suggest the possibility of coupling altermagnetism with ferroelectricity in polar chiral magnets, potentially allowing for novel mechanisms for electric-field control of magnetism. Recent theoretical studies have identified helical magnets as a platform to realize p-wave magnetism. One such material is nickel iodide (NiI2) is a van der Waals magnetic insulator and multiferroic when in its chiral magnetic phase (T < 59 K). The spin helices that characterize this phase breaks inversion symmetry, leading to a spin-induced improper charge polarization of purely electronic origin. I will introduce the intriguing properties of this material in the bulk and down to the two-dimensional limit, where it was shown that the multiferroic state is robust even in a single-layer-thick sample. I will then focus on more recent work characterizing the nonrelativistic spin splitting of electronic bands in NiI2, and its connection to symmetry and chirality. I will present a demonstration of the electrical (voltage-based) switching of chirality and consequent reversal of the momentum-space spin polarization. I will conclude with an outlook for potential applications of spin-chiral multiferroics for information storage.

2164.summary: From Structural Dynamics to Operations: Human–Machine Integration for Civil Infrastructure | Fernando Moreu | CEE 595 S - Structural Engineering Seminar Series
2164.description: From Structural Dynamics to Operations: Human–Machine Integration for Civil Infrastructure  Abstract: New human–machine interfaces, sensing technologies, and automated systems are expanding the capabilities of structural engineers. Advances in structural dynamics, computational modeling, embedded sensing, and control now enable engineers to interact with robotic systems in near real time, creating new opportunities for infrastructure inspection, structural assessment, construction, and experimental testing. This seminar presents research integrating structural dynamics and engineering operations through the design, simulation, and experimental validation of human–robot interfaces. Applications include Augmented Reality (AR) systems for infrastructure inspection and automated defect detection, where image-based measurements are translated directly into engineering quantities and presented intuitively to the inspector. New tracking and sensing approaches are also introduced for low-latency identification of nonlinear structural and mechanical systems. Building on these capabilities, human–robot interfaces are developed to allow structural engineers to interact directly with robotic systems and modify their operation based on engineering judgment and observed structural response. Immersive AR environments provide intuitive access to robot motion, sensing information, and controller parameters, enabling bidirectional communication between engineers and machines without removing the engineer from the decisionmaking process. Applications spanning structural inspection, construction, and manufacturing demonstrate how these technologies can connect algorithms with engineering operations. More broadly, this work illustrates a pathway toward human–machine integration in which sensing, dynamics, automation, and engineering judgment work together to address emerging challenges in civil infrastructure.    Bio: Fernando Moreu, PE, F. ASCE, is the Robert J. Stamm Professor of Adva

2165.summary: The Physics Colloquium: Brian Fields (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) \"Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis:  the Rise of the Elements in the Early Universe\"
2165.description: Abstract: We will give an overview of the status of big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), which describes the production of the lightest nuclei--deuterium, 3He, 4He, and 7Li--during the first three minutes of cosmic time.   This is one of the few arenas in nature where all four fundamental forces play essential roles.  Standard BBN assumes that the simplest and most robust physics is at play, combining the Standard Model of particle physics, nuclear cross-section measurements, and the neutron lifetime; this leaves only a single free parameter--the cosmic density of baryons, i.e., ordinary matter.  We will emphasize the transformative influence of cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments, which pin down the cosmic baryon density to exquisite precision.  This allows BBN to make tight predictions for the primordial light element abundances, which can be compared with observations:  for deuterium the agreement is spectacular, and for helium the agreement is excellent.  This CMB/BBN concordance marks a great success of the hot big bang, and BBN and the CMB together now sharply probe cosmology, neutrino physics, and dark matter physics at times around 1 second.  But this success is tempered by lithium observations that are significantly discrepant with BBN+CMB predictions;  we will summarize possible resolutions to this \"lithium problem.\"    Turning to 4He, we will present new observations that have achieved a leap in precision.  We will discuss the implications of these observations for cosmology and physics beyond the Standard Model.   We conclude with an outlook on future CMB, astronomical, and laboratory measurements that can better probe new physics in the early Universe, and help shed light on the solution to the lithium problem.
