2185.summary: MR Elastography of Complex Brain Mechanical Properties
2185.description: Abstract  The mechanical properties of brain tissue reflect its underlying microstructure and are sensitive markers of neurological health, but the brain is a mechanically complex organ. Its white matter is organized into aligned fiber tracts that give rise to direction-dependent stiffness, and the brain sits within the skull, suspended by meninges and cerebrospinal fluid that govern how it moves in response to external loading. Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) measures tissue viscoelasticity in vivo by imaging shear wave propagation, yet conventional approaches typically make several simplifying assumptions not appropriate for the complex mechanical behavior of the brain. In this talk I will discuss the work of my group in developing MRE methods that capture this mechanical complexity. This includes approaches for estimating anisotropic properties of white matter using multiple wave excitations and transversely isotropic inversion, enabling measurement of mechanical anisotropy along major fiber pathways. I will also present our work characterizing the skull-brain interface through measurements of relative motion and mechanical coupling, and how these properties inform models of traumatic brain injury biomechanics. Finally, I will describe how these advances in MRE acquisition and inversion extend our ability to relate brain mechanics to structure and function across the lifespan. About the Speaker  Curtis L Johnson, PhD, is an Associate Professor in the Department of Biomedical Engineering at the University of Delaware, and the Director of the Center for Biomedical and Brain Imaging. He received his PhD in Mechanical Engineering in 2013 from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. His research group develops and uses magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) to measure the integrity of the human brain through tissue mechanical properties. Dr. Johnson uses these methods to understand the structure, function, and health of the brain in different populations.

2186.summary: Soft Materials Seminar - \"Impact of dynamic covalent bond exchange on physical aging in glassy vitrimers\"
2186.description: Vitrimers have the structure as thermoset polymer while dynamic bond exchange allows for rearrangement of the polymer strands and monomers. Here, physical aging is measured to determine if bond exchange impacts glassy state vitrimers and compared to permanent analogs. Imine dynamic covalent bonds in ethylene oxide networks were prepared with linker lengths of 11, 13, and 17 backbone atoms using EO diamines and a benzene trialdehyde crosslinker. Permanent analogs used the same diamines but trimesoyl chloride. Differential scanning calorimetry was used to measure the glass transition (Tg) and enthalpy for networks aged at Tg -10°C, -15°C and -20°C for 1, 2, 5, 10 and 24 hours. Imine vitrimers show reduced aging rate compared to permanent networks for all linker lengths, with the largest difference at Tg – 20°C.
2186.location: 100 Materials Science and Engineering Building, 1304 W. Green Street

2187.summary: Soft Materials Seminar - \"Swelling-triggered stiffening through programmed topology in mechanically interlocked materials\"
2187.description: Mechanically interlocked materials (MIMs) have emerged as a promising platform for geometry- and topology-guided design, offering new opportunities for programmable mechanical response beyond those accessible in continuous materials. However, most MIMs are still fabricated from rigid solids, which limits access to dynamic functionality. Here, we introduce topology-programmed MIM platform built from toroidal mesh structures designed to encapsulate swelling-responsive materials such as hydrogels. The permeable mesh confines the hydrogel within each toroid while leaving it open to the surrounding environment. As hydrogel expansion is coupled to both mesh confinement and the interlocking constraints, swelling can stiffen the MIMs. We investigate how swelling affects contact, inter-element confinement, and collective mechanical response. The programmed topology converts local volumetric expansion into restrictions to collective motion, so the responsiveness of material sets its macroscopic stiffness. This work establishes a design strategy for integrating responsive polymer networks with architected interlocked systems, opening new opportunities for adaptive metamaterials in soft robotics, wearable protection, and tunable damping.

2194.description: Latent-Space Deep Learning for Surrogate Modeling and Bayesian Inversion with Application to Subsurface Flow and Transport Advisors: Professor Alexandre M. Tartakovsky & Professor Ximing Cai Abstract Water supply, the containment of contaminants, geothermal energy, and the geological storage of carbon dioxide all depend on predictions of flow and transport beneath the land surface. These physical processes are governed by partial differential equations (PDEs) whose coefficients, the subsurface properties such as hydraulic conductivity and porosity, vary in space and can be measured directly only at a few locations. The properties must therefore be inferred from sparse, indirect measurements of the system’s response. Bayesian inference provides the framework for this task. A prior distribution describes the geology before the data are seen, and a likelihood measures how well a candidate field reproduces the data through the PDE model. Combining the two yields the posterior distribution, which gives both the estimate and its uncertainty. Bayesian inversion is difficult in practice, because the unknown fields are described by thousands of parameters, each evaluation of the likelihood requires an expensive simulation, and realistic priors are often known only through examples. This dissertation addresses these difficulties by describing the unknown fields with a small number of latent variables and building deep-learning models in this latent space. The first part focuses on the likelihood. It defines the latent space with the Karhunen–Loève expansion, a classical statistical description of random fields, and replaces the expensive simulation with the randomized KL-DNN, a fast deep-learning surrogate that also estimates its own error. Surrogates built in this space can be transferred to new conditions by retraining only a small part of the network, and they yield posteriors that account for the uncertainty of the data, the physical model, and the surrogate itself. 2196.description: Title: The Art of Freezing Fast: Exponential Convergence in Simulated Annealing Abstract: In 1989, my family and I moved from the Australian National University to the University of Illinois, where I began my academic career. I had already heard about Bruce Hajek's remarkable research on simulated annealing, particularly his 1988 paper that continues to influence research on non-convex optimization nearly four decades later. Simulated annealing is celebrated for its convergence guarantees, but notorious for its painfully slow convergence rates. We ask in this lecture, could this apparent limitation reflect a misaligned goal? Why should an optimization algorithm be required to converge to a global optimum, rather than simply find one? Beginning with Hajek's insights we examine simulated annealing and related stochastic gradient methods through the lens of continuous-time Langevin dynamics. Theory and examples reveal that demanding convergence can make both classical simulated annealing and optimally tuned fixed-temperature methods extraordinarily slow. We then turn to a different approach: separate exploration from exploitation, and remember the best solutions discovered. One or more noisy gradient-based processes explore the landscape, searching for regions from which deterministic gradient descent can reach a global optimizer. Rather than requiring the exploring processes to converge, we ask how quickly they can discover such regions, and how effectively repeated exploration and refinement can exploit these discoveries. This viewpoint leads naturally to questions of temperature selection, restart strategies, and the design of exploration and exploitation epochs. We will discuss theoretical insights from first-hitting-time distributions, the replica-exchange approach of Dong and Tong, and recent numerical investigations of multi-temperature exploration. 2197.description: Network-Scale Geometry and Appearance-Informed Image Analysis for Pavement Friction Prediction Advisor: Professor Imad L. Al-Qadi Abstract Pavement friction is a critical surface characteristic that allows drivers to brake, accelerate, and corner safely. It is closely related to traffic safety, particularly under wet conditions. Transportation agencies measure friction and surface texture that controls it to identify locations requiring traction restoration. However, existing friction measurement equipment, including high-speed laser scanners, are expensive to purchase and operate, produce sporadic measurements, have limited lane coverage, and require significant training and maintenance. As a result, frequent deployment at the network level may be infeasible for transportation agencies, which further exacerbates safety risks. To overcome these challenges, a scalable and relatively inexpensive vision-based setup was proposed for contactless identification of pavement surface texture and friction. The setup captures raw sensor data at speeds up to 56 km/hr (35 mi/hr), produces high-resolution 3D point clouds of pavement surfaces, and infers the friction coefficient based on macrotexture data and other roadway features. An image-based 3D reconstruction framework based on Structure from Motion (SfM) was developed. Imaging equipment like Digital Single Lens Reflux (DSLR) and action cameras were used to capture pavement surface photos. Parameters such as capture heigh, camera orientation, and image overlap were evaluated to maximize point cloud quality and resolution. The point cloud scale ambiguity was resolved by including ground control points in the captured scene and by georeferencing images using a Real Time Kinematics (RTK) Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receiver. 2202.description: Modeling Human Interventions to Understand Streamflow Changes and Water Management Implications in River Basins Advisor: Professor Ximing Cai Abstract Hydrological models support improved understanding of hydrological processes, forecasts of extreme events, water availability assessments, and evaluations of climate and land use change impacts. The credibility of these outputs greatly depends on how accurately hydrological models represent human water management. Despite substantial efforts on improving human representations, data limitations have required simplifying assumptions, which introduces biases and obscures model-based inferences. This dissertation improves the representation and evaluation of human water management in hydrological models to understand human effects on streamflow and water availability at the river basin scale. We start with streamflow regulation by reservoirs and examine if more realistic reservoir representation in a watershed hydrologic model can generate more accurate streamflow simulations. Five reservoir representations are coupled with a conceptual rainfall-runoff model to evaluate watershed outflow, internal fluxes, and model parameters. The results show two representations derived from long-term reservoir operation records improve not only the watershed outflow but also the internal flux (reservoir inflow) across five watersheds. The identified reservoir representations are included in a national-scale data inventory of human interventions in hydrological systems (Data_IH2) that we compile to conduct basin-scale impact analysis of multiple human activities. Data_IH2 encompasses reservoir operations, irrigation, drainage, stormwater management, inter-basin transfers, and water supplies. We also develop a diagnostic framework to evaluate the utility of Data_IH2 in large-scale hydrological models without calibration and parameterization biases. 2203.summary: Hard Materials Seminar - \"Molten salts and nuclear reactors: a matter of chemistry\"
2203.description: Due to their advantageous thermophysical and neutronic properties, molten salts are proposed in a variety of roles across advanced fission (both fast and thermal spectrum) and fusion reactors (both inertial and magnetic confinement) to help achieve high operating temperatures, intrinsic safety, and improved economics in power generation. In all these systems, the chemical behavior of molten salts is crucial towards reactor design needs such as corrosion mitigation, tritium management, on-line sensing, chemistry control. This talk will provide an introduction on molten salt chemistry, discussing how molten salt physical and chemical properties affect their behavior in nuclear reactors, providing examples of the outstanding chemistry and materials challenges, and describing how the Advanced Blankets & Coolants Lab at UIUC is working towards addressing them.

Dr. Zhang’s research interests focus on characterizing climate-related exposures, reducing the human health effects associated with disasters, and exploring the role of social and environmental stressors (air pollution, natural environment, built environment, and green space) in relation to chronic diseases. Dr. Zhang currently serves as the Secretary of the International Society of Exposure Science (ISES) and a standing member of NIH Social and Environmental Determinants of Health Study Section. He is also an Associate Editor for Journal of Hazardous Materials, Science of the Total Environment, and the Journal of Exposure Science and Environmental Epidemiology. 2213.summary: ISE Seminar Series - Dr. Jackie Cha
2213.description: Title: Human-Robot Collaborations in Surgery: Measuring Skills, Demands, and Safety  Abstract: The widespread adoption of surgical robotic systems in the operating room has fundamentally reshaped how surgical team members physically and cognitively interact with both technology and one another. This shift has highlighted the need to reconsider nontechnical skills – task-relevant cognitive and interpersonal skills among surgical team members – and to reassess the physical demands placed on clinicians throughout a procedure. This presentation will describe sensor-based measures of nontechnical skills in robotic-assisted surgery, drawing on behavioral and physiological metrics collected from surgical teams to characterize communication, coordination, and workload. It will also present findings from live and simulated procedures on the physical demands of surgery, highlighting conditions in which arm- and shoulder-support exoskeletons reduce those demands for surgeons and perioperative staff. Collectively, this work is aimed at improving surgical human-robot collaborations and team dynamics to promote clinician and patient safety, surgical performance, and the overall quality of surgical care.  Bio: Dr. Jackie Cha is the Patricia Flatley Brennan Assistant Professor in the Department of Industrial and Systems Engineering at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, with an affiliate appointment in Biomedical Engineering. Her research focuses on measuring physical and cognitive human-robot interactions, particularly in healthcare environments, to improve worker performance, safety, and system efficiency. Her group investigates applications of robotics – both surgical robotic systems and wearables – in clinical environments and the changes of physical and cognitive interactions between human teams and robots. Prior to joining UW-Madison, she served as an assistant professor at Clemson University. She obtained her PhD in Industrial Engineering from Purdue University and MSE/BSE

2220.summary: AE 590 Seminar Speaker: Sedina Tsikata - Stability and Time-Resolved Dynamics of Fluctuations in Magnetized Electric Propulsion Plasmas
2220.description: Abstract: Magnetized electric propulsion plasmas exhibit broadband, multiscale fluctuations that influence cross-field transport and discharge dynamics. Although significant progress has been made in identifying the underlying instabilities, their temporal evolution and interactions remain difficult to characterize from frequency spectra alone. This work examines two complementary approaches to understanding fluctuation dynamics and stability. First, dispersion relation analysis is used to investigate unstable wave branches and growth rates under conditions relevant to an applied-field magnetoplasmadynamic thruster prototype. The analysis identifies potentially unstable modes accessible to non-invasive diagnostics and examines their sensitivity to plasma parameters, particularly the applied magnetic field. Second, time-resolved coherent Thomson scattering measurements in a Hall thruster are analyzed to characterize the statistical and phase dynamics of electron density fluctuations at selected spatial scales. Analysis of isolated spectral modes examines their amplitude, instantaneous frequency, frequency wandering, and phase coherence over successive time windows. The results reveal evolving fluctuation states in which mode amplitude, frequency, and phase organization do not necessarily vary together. In particular, substantial fluctuation amplitudes can persist as phase coherence decreases, while frequency drift and enhanced frequency variability accompany changes in mode organization.  Together, these approaches illustrate how linear stability analysis and time-resolved statistical diagnostics can provide complementary insights into instability-driven fluctuations, their nonlinear evolution, and their potential implications for transport in magnetized electric propulsion plasmas. Bio: Sedina Tsikata is an Associate Professor in Aerospace Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology. Her research concerns the fundamental nature and applications of magnetized

2221.summary: Hassel and Marianne Ledbetter MatSE Colloquium - \"Wearable ultrasound technology\"
2221.description: The use of wearable electronic devices that can acquire vital signs from the human body noninvasively and continuously is a significant trend for healthcare. The combination of materials design and advanced microfabrication techniques enables the integration of various components and devices onto a wearable platform, resulting in functional systems with minimal limitations on the human body. Physiological signals from deep tissues are particularly valuable as they have a stronger and faster correlation with the internal events within the body compared to signals obtained from the surface of the skin. In this presentation, I will demonstrate a soft ultrasonic technology that can noninvasively and continuously acquire dynamic information about deep tissues and central organs. I will also showcase examples of this technology's use in recording blood pressure and flow waveforms in central vessels, monitoring cardiac chamber activities, and measuring core body temperatures. The soft ultrasonic technology presented represents a platform with vast potential for applications in consumer electronics, defense medicine, and clinical practices.

2225.summary: CHBE 565-Thomas J. Hanratty Lecture, Prof. Timothy P. Lodge, University of Minnesota (Host: Prof. Alexa Kuenstler) \"Spontaneous Fission and Fusion of Block Copolymer Micelles\"
2225.description: Abstract:  Block copolymers provide a remarkably versatile platform for achieving desired nanostructures by self-assembly, with dimensions ranging from a few nanometers up to microns. In particular, block copolymer micelles in selective solvents are of interest across a range of technologies, including drug delivery, imaging, catalysis, lubrication, and extraction. While block copolymers generally adopt the morphologies familiar in small molecule surfactants and lipids (i.e., spherical micelles, worm-like micelles, and vesicles), one key difference is that polymeric micelles are typically not at equilibrium. This is a result of strong segregation; the length of the core-forming block, coupled to a large interfacial tension, make it difficult for changes to re-arrange once micelles are formed. The kinetic barriers involved can easily approach 100 kBT. When micelles are significantly larger or smaller than the equilibrium size, fission and fusion mechanisms, respectively, can become operative. We will describe measurements using dynamic light scattering, small-angle X-ray scattering, and liquid-phase TEM to follow both processes in detail, with some remarkable and unexpected results. For example, the data suggest that fission proceeds through a metastable intermediate state, which is not anticipated by theory. Fusion is “quantized”, in the sense that a population of micelles completely undergoes one fusion event to double the average aggregation number, before a second or third event takes place, suggesting that the rate constant for fusion is a strongly decreasing function of micelle size. In order for fusion to be observed, it is necessary to reduce the steric barrier provided by the corona chains, which can be achieved by systematically reducing the solvent quality for the corona block. 2227.summary: Adapting to Cracks: Learning from the Dynamic Structure of Mineralized Tissues and Cells
2227.description: Abstract  Biogenic materials such as bone exhibit a combination of properties exceeding that of their constituents, a feat generally credited to their hierarchical structure, down to the nanoscale, where mineralized collagen fibrils act as the mechanical building blocks. Because of this inherent nanometer scale, we have limited knowledge of bone’s time-dependent and small-scale response to physiological loading. During cyclic loading, injury, and repair, bone tissue is exposed to large strains and dynamic loads, a drastic departure from the quasi-static, macroscale conditions on which our current knowledge of bone fracture is based. Here, we will use in situ electron and X-ray nanomechanical experiments to ask: How does the nanostructure of bone respond to cyclic physiological loading? What mechanisms dictate dynamic fracture? And how do the cells embedded in bone sense and respond to these dynamic changes? Finally, we will show how nano and metal additive manufacturing let us both probe these questions and translate bone’s design principles into fatigue-resistant synthetic materials. About the Speaker  Ottman Tertuliano is the AMA Family Assistant Professor in Mechanical Engineering and Applied Mechanics (MEAM) at Penn, where he leads research exploring how mechanical forces shape both natural tissues and engineered materials. By uncovering how physiological loads influence tissue health and resilience, his group designs synthetic systems with similar adaptability—structural materials that adapt and endure under changing demands. Ottman’s group leverages this bio-inspired approach to develop biocompatible materials that guide cellular behavior while advancing additive manufacturing for synthetic materials that achieve improved “material health” over time. Ottman earned his B.S. in Mechanical Engineering from Columbia University in 2013 and a Ph.D. in Materials Science from Caltech in 2018, where he specialized in nanoscale studies of bone mechanics and fracture. 2228.summary: Soft Materials Seminar - \"Design, Fabrication and Mechanical Testing of Photo-Patterned Semi-Crystalline Materials\"
2228.description: In this study, we fabricated poly(1,5-cyclooctadiene) [p(COD)] using Ring-Opening Metathesis Polymerization (ROMP) with a thermally activated catalyst and used light to control the crystallinity. However, after polymerization, residual active initiator and chain ends undergo secondary metathesis. This can cause cis-to-trans double bond conversion causing the crystallinity to evolve over time affecting the mechanical properties. To address this, we investigated a method for deactivating the catalyst and preventing the progression of increasing crystallinity over time. By using a photo-based generator that when activated releases a base that prevents further metathesis. By varying light intensity and exposure time we can create distinct regions with varying crystallinity, which allows us to create any predefined pattern on the structures. Specimens were fabricated incorporating patterns such as lizard scales, circular hexagonal packing array, and vertically aligned lamellae. Non-patterned samples were used as a benchmark and were irradiated at 0 hours, 24 hours or 72 hours. Samples were subjected to uniaxial tension, and we used digital image correlation (DIC) to capture the fully localized strain field. We observed non-homogenous variation in the localized strain for the patterned materials, whereas non-patterned samples displayed a homogenous localized strain. Through controlling light intensity and pattern type during fabrication, we can induce mechanical gradient properties in materials and locally tune the strain distribution of polymeric materials. Using light to develop complex high-resolution patterns enables exact predesign of polymeric materials. In this present work, we investigated a novel fabrication technique for patterned structures and DIC supported mechanical characterization allowed us to have a deeper understanding of the mechanical behaviors of the patterned samples at multi-scale length.
2228.location: 100 Materials Science and Engineering Building, 1304 W. Green Street

2229.summary: Soft Materials Seminar - \"Synthesis and Characterization of Polycatenated DNA Crystals\"
2229.description: Mechanically interlocked structures exhibit behaviors distinct from those of continuous materials because their properties emerge from geometry and topology in addition to chemical composition. Polycatenated architectures, such as chainmail, are especially attractive because they provide flexibility, rigidity, and reconfigurability. Although topological constraints have been studied at the macroscale and in molecular machines, the precise realization of interlocked 3D lattice structures at the nanoscale remains a major synthetic challenge.    Here, we present the bottom-up self-assembly of nanoscale polycatenated architected materials (nano-PAMs) using DNA origami. By combining the structural programmability of DNA origami with nanoparticle-templated assembly, we synthesize and characterize highly ordered polycatenated lattices with designed spatial symmetries. Specifically, we demonstrate the assembly of 3D crystalline superlattices through the site-selective interlocking of DNA origami-based topological motifs. We further establish the versatility of this synthetic strategy by systematically designing the geometries of the DNA origami building blocks and templating nanoparticles to access a diverse set of nano-PAM structures.    Furthermore, using nano-PAM as a model system, we seek to investigate the unusual thermal behavior inherent to mechanically interlocked colloidal crystals by probing temperature-dependent changes in order mainly driven by thermal fluctuations. By rationally programming the degree of structural order at the nanoscale, these architectures could enable spatial templating of various materials to modulate their resultant photonic, mechanical, phononic, and acoustic behaviors. More broadly, this design paradigm establishes a versatile platform for constructing nano-PAMs with tunable properties, opening opportunities for stimuli-responsive and reconfigurable nanoscale systems.
2229.location: 100 Materials Science and Engineering Building, 1304 W. Green Street

2239.summary: CHBE 565-International Paper Co Seminar-Prof. Amanda Marciel, Rice University (Host: Prof. Simon Rogers) \"Influence of Block Length and Tacticity on Polyampholyte Conformation and Phase Behavior\"
2239.description: Bio: Amanda B. Marciel is an Assistant Professor and William Marsh Rice Trustee Chair of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at Rice University. She earned a B.S. in Chemical Biology from the University of California at Berkeley in 2008 and Ph.D. in Biophysics from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign with Professor Charles M. Schroeder in 2015. She worked at the Institute for Molecular Engineering (IME) at The University of Chicago as a Postdoctoral Fellow with Professor Matthew V. Tirrell. The Marciel group investigates how monomer chemistry and sequence influence the behavior of charged polymers in solution and at interfaces to design stimuli-responsive materials. Abstract: In this work, we investigate the effect of the charge-block length on the chain conformation and phase behavior of peptide polyampholytes (PAs) with equal numbers of cationic and anionic ionizable monomers. Peptide PAs were produced using solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), which enables precise control of the molecular weight, monomer sequence, and chain tacticity. Using circular dichroism (CD) and Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, we observe that the atactic peptide PAs show no evidence of secondary structure formation regardless of block length, whereas isotactic peptide PAs exhibit block-length-dependent secondary structures. Turbidity measurements show that the isotactic peptide PAs phase separate with increasing block length. In contrast, the atactic peptide PAs remain in solution over a wide-range of salt concentrations.  Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) measurements reveal that the chain conformation of peptide PAs is compressed compared to expectations for neutral systems. Interestingly, we find that the atactic peptide PAs form block-length-dependent multichain clusters in solution. These results are consistent with a recent theory predicting that PAs have a block-length- and concentration-dependent threshold for phase separation.

2241.summary: Hard Materials Seminar - \"Developing a High-Throughput Test Method for Corrosion in Bio-Feedstocks\"
2241.description: Bio-based feedstocks and fuels are strong candidates for replacing petroleum, but the corrosion resistance of metals in bio-feedstocks is not well understood, which slows the adoption of biofuels. These bio-feedstocks contain more oxygen than petroleum and often have more complex bio-molecules and compositions. This oxygen content results in a higher corrosivity, and this complexity results in a larger variable space to test. Traditional corrosion immersion tests and electrochemical methods are difficult to use at the high temperatures and pressures present in refineries. They also do not scale well to test a large array of bio-feedstock solutions or constituents. In this talk, we will present a new high-throughput immersion method using custom reaction vessels. We will discuss our factorial experiments testing some of the key vessel design parameters and the method’s repeatability. By controlling these parameters, we aim to refine this test method and begin studying the mechanism of corrosion by bio-feedstocks.

2244.description: TITLE: Ditch the Distribution: ETAs for Truck Scheduling  ABSTRACT: Logistics synchronization problems often require coordinating vehicles with resources at their destinations. Uncertain travel times complicate this coordination. Existing models typically assume known travel time distributions and no new information about travel times until vehicles reach their destinations. In practice, navigation systems provide operators with frequent estimated times of arrival (ETAs), creating opportunities to improve synchronization through real-time information. Motivated by our collaboration with the logistics division of the Italian post, we study inbound truck scheduling at warehouse unloading docks with frequent ETA updates. We formulate the problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) that represents arrival uncertainty through belief distributions updated with each ETA. We develop a lookahead policy for dynamic resource allocation under evolving ETA information. To evaluate the policy, we derive an information relaxation dual bound, which yields a challenging penalized perfect information problem. We develop a decomposition algorithm that separates truck-to-dock assignment and sequencing from service start time decisions. Experiments show that the dual bound substantially improves upon conventional perfect information bounds, the lookahead policy achieves near-optimal performance when arrival time distributions are known, and incorporating ETAs reduces expected waiting time by 29 percent relative to current industry practice.  BIO: Justin Goodson is a professor at Saint Louis University. He researches methods to solve sequential decision problems. He teaches analytics, supply chain management, and reinforcement learning. He studied business analytics and industrial engineering at the University of Iowa and the University of Missouri. He enjoys photography, writing, and musical composition.

2270.description: Title: Moving Lifelines: Fixed Sites or Mobile Fleets for Volunteer-Enabled Emergency Medical Device Delivery?  Abstract: Timely use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, yet AED deployment creates value only if devices reach patients within a clinical window. We study how a city should allocate an AED budget between fixed locations and mobile fleets to maximize timely deliveries. In the fixed-location (static) system, a responder retrieves an AED before reaching the patient; in the mobile system, on-demand fleet vehicles carry AEDs for direct delivery. We develop a stochastic spatial model capturing two-leg static retrieval and mobile fleet idleness. We first characterize both pure systems. Static performance depends jointly on AED and responder density: increasing either resource eventually yields a ceiling determined by the other. Mobile deployment avoids this retrieval-geometry bottleneck, but fleet idleness and driver responsiveness discount each AED-equipped vehicle’s value. Across otherwise comparable cities, a larger population increases responder density but reduces mobile fleet idleness, producing a unique switch in the preferred pure system from mobile to static. Under identifiable conditions, small budgets can make static deployment inferior even with arbitrarily dense responders. We then solve the joint allocation problem. A log-miss reformulation reveals a scale effect of static deployment, whereas each mobile AED contributes a constant log-miss reduction. Optimal policies therefore concentrate AEDs in one channel until a channel-specific limit makes hybrid deployment relevant. Computable thresholds characterize these regimes. Using real-world data, we find that, at observed AED stocks, the calibrated model favors pure static deployment in New York City and pure mobile deployment in Singapore.  Short Bio: Jingwei Zhang is an Assistant Professor of Operations, Technology, and Informat

2277.summary: AE 590 Seminar Speaker: Ivan Bermejo-Moreno - Large-eddy simulation of transonic buffet with wind-tunnel confinement effects
2277.description: Abstract: Transonic airfoil buffet of a supercritical OAT15A airfoil at Mach 0.72 and an angle of attack of 5º is studied with high-fidelity numerical simulations that aim to replicate wind-tunnel experiments conducted at the Trisonic Wind Tunnel of the Institute of Aerodynamics, RWTH Aachen University. Large-eddy simulations with and without an equilibrium wall model, as well as different spanwise domain length and boundary treatments are performed to assess the effects of wind-tunnel confinement (from the top/bottom and side walls) on the observed buffet-cycle dynamics, including oscillatory lambda-shock motion, shock-induced separation, and wake vortex shedding. Comparisons with Schlieren and particle-image velocimetry (PIV) experimental measurements will be presented, including modal analyses employing spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) techniques. Bio: Ivan Bermejo-Moreno is an associate professor in the Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering Department of the Viterbi School of Engineering at the University of Southern California. He received an Aeronautical Engineer degree from the Polytechnic University of Madrid, Spain, followed by M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees in aeronautics from the California Institute of Technology. Afterwards, he held a postdoctoral research fellowship at the Center for Turbulence Research, Stanford University/NASA Ames Research Center. His research combines numerical methods, physical modeling, and high-performance computing for the simulation and analysis of turbulent fluid flows involving multi-physics phenomena. Prof. Bermejo-Moreno is an Associate Fellow of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, and the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, the NASA Early Career Faculty Award, the Fulbright Fellowship, the Rolf D. Buhler Memorial Award, the William F. Ballhaus Prize, and the Hans G. Hornung Prize.

2314.description: Join Illini Union Board for an  Evening with Olympic gold medalist Shawn Johnson East on Tuesday, Nov. 10, at 7 p.m. at Foellinger Auditorium. Students can submit questions for Shawn, enter for a chance to participate in the post-event meet and greet, or share accessibility and accommodation needs through the event form. After retiring from gymnastics in 2012, Olympic gold medalist Shawn Johnson East has continued to build an impressive career as an author, broadcaster, entrepreneur and media personality. Her accomplishments include becoming a New York Times best-selling author, winning “Dancing with the Stars” and launching several businesses alongside her husband, former NFL player Andrew East. Together, Shawn and Andrew connect with more than 13.8 million followers across social media, host a YouTube channel with more than 1 billion views and produce a New York Times-praised podcast that has reached No. 1 on the overall charts. During the 2024 Paris Olympics, Shawn served as a gymnastics expert and correspondent for Yahoo! Sports. She later won FOX’s “Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test” and was named to Adweek’s 2025 Most Powerful Women in Sports list. 2467.description: Let M be a closed hyperbolic 3-manifold and epsilon>0. We will show that the number (1+epsilon)-quasifuchsian surfaces of genus at most g in M, up to homotopy and common finite covers, grows like g^{2g}. We will then use this to obtain a modified version of the minimal surface entropy rigidity theorem of Calegari, Marques, and Neves. This is joint work with Franco Vargas Pallete and Jia Wan.

2468.description: TITLE: Subspaces and quotients of $L_1$ defined by subsequences of the Haar system ABSTRACT: Consider the closed subspace of $L_1[0,1]$ spanned by the even (respectively, odd) levels of the Haar system. In $L_p$, $1 < p < \infty$, and dyadic $H^1$, the spaces spanned by subsequences of the Haar system were completely characterized by Gamlen-Gaudet and Müller, respectively. However, in $L_1$ it has remained open whether the spans of the even or odd levels are isomorphic to $L_1$. We give a negative answer, based on absolutely 2-summing operators: neither subspace is isomorphic to $L_1$. Moreover, we show that the quotient of $L_1$ by the closed span of any subsequence of the Haar system has cotype 2, which also implies cotype 2 for the transportation cost spaces on diamond graphs. The cotype results are joint work with Stephen Dilworth, Denka Kutzarova, and Mikhail Ostrovskii. OpenAI’s ChatGPT 6.0 Astra was used in obtaining the above results.

2469.summary: Concentration after a Contracting Experiment: Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation
2469.description: Abstract: Policymakers occasionally intervene to reduce concentration in a market; the EU’s 2014 mandatory audit firm rotation (MFR) regulation is a prominent example. One objective of MFR was to erode the Big 4’s dominance by forcing periodic auditor switches for public companies. However, heterogeneous firm-level demand for auditor-specific expertise may cause companies to rotate within rather than away from the Big 4, leaving overall concentration unchanged. We formalize this intuition in a theoretical matching model whereby large clients re-sort to the Big 4 under forced rotation, so that mandatory switching churns engagements within the dominant tier rather than dispersing them. We test the prediction by evaluating the EU regulatory change as a quasi-experiment, using the US—which did not adopt it—as a control. We find, within tight bounds, that MFR did not reduce the fee-weighted market share of the Big 4: the policymaker’s concentration reduction objective was not achieved. The flow decomposition of auditor switches shows that 95.4% of the post-MFR fee volume that rotates does so without crossing the Big 4 boundary, with the firms that do cross being small and fee-immaterial. MFR thus redirects rather than removes concentration.

2470.description: Title: Introduction to Loop Measures II: Loop-Erased Random Walks and Spanning Trees Abstract: In the previous talk, we introduced rooted and unrooted loop measures, their generating functions, and loop soups. In this talk, we will explore the connection between loop measures and spanning trees through loop-erased random walks. We will first introduce chronological loop erasure and derive a formula for the weights of loop-erased paths in terms of loop measures. We will then discuss Wilson's algorithm for generating spanning trees and show how it produces a uniform spanning tree on a finite connected graph. Reference: Lawler, G. F., & Limic, V. (2010). Random Walk: A Modern Introduction, Sections 9.5 and 9.7. Cambridge University Press.

2476.summary: DATE CHANGE: Philosophy Colloquium Lecture Series: Graham Oddie, University of Colorado
2476.description: Parity at Risk Things could be worse. Things could also be better. Or they could be exactly equally good. But could things be neither worse, nor better, nor equally good? There are interesting arguments for that possibility. If two things do not instantiate any of the three standard value relations we might conclude that they are simply incomparable for value. But there may be another possibility—a fourth genuinely comparative  value relation— parity. Things that are on a par do not instantiate any of the three standard value relations but they are (in a sense which will be made precise) still comparable for value. We start with a fundamental value relation, at least as good, and provide an analysis of parity, distinguishing it from brute incomparability.  We then show that within a probabilistic framework the parity postulate entails some rather unpalatable consequences involving risky alternatives. This paper is jointly authored  by Graham Oddie  and Gustaf Arrhenius (Institute for Futures Studies, Stockholm). Oddie is emeritus professor of philosophy at the University of Colorado, and Arrhenius is professor of philosophy at the University of Stockholm.) Oddie will give the presentation

2483.description: The Kodachrome revolution: idealizations and understanding for stratospheric cooling with increasing CO2 and the role of clouds in a greenhouse atmosphereThe combination of deep understanding of the physics controlling the flow of radiation though the atmosphere, increasingly detailed characterization of atmospheric state,  and rapidly-expanding computational capabilities, has enabled ever-more-accurate calculations of radiation balance over the last decades. These computations underlie many of our expectations about the future including stratospheric cooling in response to increasing CO2 levels and more precipitation from a warming atmosphere… but they don’t tell us why these phenomena emerge. I will describe how the three key idealizations underlying the Kodachrome revolution - of spectroscopy, of radiative transfer, and of constraints imposed by the condensability of water vapor - are driving rapid progress in understanding a wide range of behavior. I’ll show how the enormous spectral variation of absorption by water vapor and carbon dioxide are responsible  a) for the cooling of the stratosphere and the resulting increase in top-of-atmosphere imbalance as CO2 concentrations are increased and b) for the surprising influence of water vapor and carbon dioxide on the radiation budget in fully cloudy skies.   https://illinois.zoom.us/j/87247933909?pwd=Yg9a5afZrUDAodWJBhap3HvxzMVVeo.1 Meeting ID: 872 4793 3909     Pass Code: 202496

Whether you're looking to strengthen your quantitative skills or advance your expertise in modern statistical methods, our programs provide a rigorous and flexible curriculum, with opportunities to tailor your coursework to your career goals.  During the info session, you’ll have the chance to:Learn about our MS in Statistics, MS in Analytics, and other program optionsGain insights into the application process, admissions requirements, and key deadlinesDiscover the resources and support available to graduate students, including professional development, networking, and internship opportunitiesThere will also be a Q&A session where you can ask questions and learn more about how our programs align with your academic and professional aspirations. Don’t miss this chance to explore how a graduate degree in statistics from Illinois can help shape your future!

2604.description: Returning residents who have been randomly assigned a date and time for Housing Sign-Up Self-Assignment will receive information about the process on November 4. Self-Assignment will begin in the Resident Portal on Monday, November 9 at noon. Returning residents must complete the fall 2027-spring 2028 academic year contract no later than 11:59 p.m. CST on November 15. Residents will have 14 days from the time they submit their contract to cancel their Housing contract without incurring a contract cancellation fee. Note: Residents who do not complete the process in time will need to add themselves to the waitlist.

He has taught art at the collegiate level since 2001 and currently teaches drawing at McHenry County College

2714.description: The night sky has been the subject of campfire stories, ancient myths and awe for as long as there have been people. A desire to comprehend the Universe may well be humanity’s oldest shared intellectual experience. Yet only recently have we truly begun to grasp our place in the vast cosmos. To learn about this journey of celestial discovery, from the theories of the ancient Greek astronomers to today’s grandest telescopes, we invite you to experience From Earth to the Universe, a new fulldome sh

2715.description: While Celeste is fighting off sleep in her room by reading a book on astronomy she receives an unexpected visit from Moon. Together, they will enjoy a journey through the Universe to discover what exoplanets are and how they can be detected. They observe rogue planets, oceanic worlds and super-Earths. Moon tells her about exoplanet hunters, who observe the sky in search of planets like Earth.
